YesWiki CalcField eval() RCE: php/apache web process spawns shell or recon binary AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-52778 execution phase where a bypass of the CalcField.php regex sandbox reaches eval() and runs OS commands (PoC: abs(1) + system('id')). A PHP-FPM/Apache worker forking /bin/sh, id, whoami, uname, curl or wget is the tell that the math parser was weaponised into command execution as www-data. Rationale: Directly models the article's RCE PoC (abs(1) + system('id')) — a web interpreter (php-fpm/apache) is the parent and the child is a shell/recon binary; the parent constraint is what turns generic 'id ran' into a high-fidelity CVE-2026-52778 signal. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8 • https://www.thehackerwire.com/yeswiki-rce-redos-in-bazar-calcfield-cve-2026-52778/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A YesWiki/PHP plugin legitimately shelling out to ImageMagick (convert) or ffmpeg for media processing
  • Backup or cron jobs run under the www-data account invoking bash wrapper scripts
  • CI/deploy tooling on the web host running composer post-install hooks that fork sh
  • Monitoring agents that php-exec 'uname'/'whoami' for host inventory
  • Webhook handlers that legitimately call curl/wget to fetch remote resources
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ImageMagick","convert ","ffmpeg") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "composer")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alerting host — confirm the php-fpm/apache parent's InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the child ProcessCommandLine; look for 'id','uname','curl' with no matching application feature. Correlate the timestamp with web access logs for a Bazar form-save request. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending php-fpm worker, and block the source IP at the WAF; take the YesWiki instance offline pending patch to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: on the same host search for new .php files in the webroot (webshell), www-data reads of /etc/passwd or .env, and outbound connections from php-fpm to attacker infrastructure.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","python","python3","perl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","python","python3","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki post-RCE credential access: web user reads /etc/passwd or .env AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-52778 credential-access follow-on where code running as www-data reads local secret/identity files (/etc/passwd, .env, config.php, id_rsa) as called out in the advisory's impact section. Pivots on a PHP/Apache web process whose child command line references those secret paths. Rationale: Uses the advisory's explicit credential-access impact ("read sensitive system files e.g. /etc/passwd, .env") anchored to a web-server parent process, so it only fires when the web tier — not a legitimate admin shell — touches those secrets. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A YesWiki bootstrap that legitimately reads its own config.php/.env at startup via an exec wrapper
  • Admin troubleshooting a permissions issue by grepping /etc/passwd while su'd to www-data
  • Backup scripts run as www-data that archive the app directory including .env
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet) runs touching /etc/passwd under the web user context
  • Security scanners fingerprinting the host that read /etc/passwd
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("backup","rsync","tar -") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is genuinely php-fpm/apache (not an interactive admin shell) and inspect the exact file path read; check whether the same session also spawned recon binaries (UC1). 2) Contain: rotate any credentials in the exposed files (.env DB creds, SSH keys), isolate the host, and patch YesWiki to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: search auth logs and cloud sign-ins for use of the leaked credentials, and look for webshell drops and outbound C2 from the same host.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow",".env","config.php","id_rsa","wakka.config.php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc

YesWiki webshell persistence: php/apache worker writes .php under Bazar webroot AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-52778 persistence step where the attacker uses eval() RCE to write a PHP backdoor into the YesWiki webroot (advisory: "modify application files, inject backdoors"). Fires when a PHP-FPM/Apache process creates or modifies a .php/.phtml file under the bazar/tools/yeswiki directories. Rationale: Anchored on the advisory's persistence impact ("inject backdoors") and the affected component path tools/bazar — a web worker (not a deploy pipeline) writing new .php files into its own served directory is a classic webshell drop. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • YesWiki's own Twig/template compile cache writing generated .php files under cache/ or tmp/
  • A legitimate in-app plugin/theme installer that unpacks .php files to the webroot
  • Admin-driven git pull / rsync deploy that runs as the web user and updates .php files
  • Composer autoload regeneration writing vendor .php files
  • WordPress/other CMS co-hosted on the same box writing plugin files
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/cache/","/tmp/","/twig","/vendor/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written file — a short file with eval/base64_decode/assert/system or $_POST/$_GET handlers confirms a webshell; compare its hash against known-good YesWiki files. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the file, isolate the host, block the source IP, and preserve a copy for forensics; patch to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: grep the whole webroot for other recently-modified .php files, check web access logs for GET/POST hits to the new path, and review UC1/UC2 for the initial command execution and secret theft.

| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".php5"
| where FolderPath has_any ("bazar","/tools/","yeswiki")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

YesWiki CVE-2026-52778 exploit request: Bazar formula with system() or nested-paren ReDoS AIDelivery Low
Hunts the initial-access/exploit HTTP request to a YesWiki Bazar CalcField carrying either the RCE marker system( or the deeply nested-parenthesis structure used for the PCRE stack-overflow DoS. Web-tier hunting query; grounded in the advisory's two PoC payloads. Rationale: Both PoC payloads from the advisory are used verbatim — the RCE string system( and the thousands-of-nested-parens ReDoS structure (matched as 6+ consecutive '('). Scoped to Bazar to cut noise; low confidence because the payload often lives in the POST body rather than the URL (false negatives), so pair with UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778 • https://www.thehackerwire.com/yeswiki-rce-redos-in-bazar-calcfield-cve-2026-52778/ • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Bazar Calc field with a genuinely paren-heavy but valid math formula
  • Security scanners / DAST tooling probing the YesWiki instance with fuzz payloads
  • A WAF that URL-decodes and logs POST bodies producing benign 'system(' substrings in unrelated content
  • Copy-pasted formula documentation submitted through the form
  • Load-testing tools replaying recorded Bazar save requests
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request (method, source IP, authenticated user, body if captured) and the HTTP status — a 5xx or dropped connection alongside a huge nested-paren body indicates a successful ReDoS crash; a 200 with system( suggests RCE attempt. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, add a rule rejecting Bazar formula fields exceeding a sane length / paren depth, and prioritise patching to YesWiki >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: on the target host correlate with UC1 (php spawning shell), php-fpm worker segfaults/restarts in syslog, and new webshell files (UC3) from the same source IP or session.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "bazar"
| where Url contains "system(" or Url matches regex @"\({6,}"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki BazarImport POST exploit request (CVE-2026-52777) — vue=importer + base64 importfiche payload AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound POST requests to the YesWiki BazaR importer route (`?BazaR&vue=importer&id_typeannonce=N`) carrying the `importfiche[0]` parameter with a base64-encoded serialized-PHP blob. This is the exact CSRF-delivered exploitation vector for the unauthenticated-in-practice PHP Object Injection sink `unserialize(base64_decode($entry))` in CSVManager.php. Rationale: Uses the article's exact route (`?BazaR&vue=importer&id_typeannonce=`) and `importfiche` source parameter — the importer POST is an admin-rare operation, so any POST to it is high-fidelity; where WAF body logging exists, additionally match `importfiche` + a >=50-char base64 blob (PHP-serialized base64 begins `YT`/`Tzo`). Cross-checked PHPGGC and YesWiki Bazar RCE history. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/issues/356 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-88xg-v53p-fpvf • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778
ATT&CKT1190 T1027
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate wiki administrator using the Bazar CSV import UI to bulk-load entries
  • Automated content-migration scripts that call the importer endpoint
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing the endpoint post-disclosure
  • Penetration-test engagement replaying the PoC curl request
  • Backup/restore tooling that re-imports Bazar form data
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the full request for the flagged hit — confirm csMethod=POST to the importer route and inspect the body (via WAF) for an `importfiche[0]=` base64 blob; base64-decode it and check for a serialized-object marker (`O:` / class names like Doctrine). Note source IP and whether csUserName is a real admin. 2) CONTAIN: block the source IP at the WAF, invalidate the implicated admin session/cookie, and confirm YesWiki is upgraded to >= 4.6.6 (patched). 3) HUNT: pivot to the web host and check for php-fpm/apache spawning a shell and for new `.php`/`wakka.config.php` writes within minutes of the request (UC3/UC4).
W3CIISLog

| where csUriQuery has "BazaR" and csUriQuery has "vue=importer"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csUserName, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cross-site (CSRF) POST to YesWiki BazaR importer — off-origin/absent Referer AIDelivery Medium
Detects the CSRF delivery mechanism specific to CVE-2026-52777: an admin's browser auto-POSTs to `?BazaR&vue=importer` from attacker-controlled HTML, so the Referer host differs from the wiki host (or is stripped). The article confirms the importentries branch invokes NO CsrfTokenController::checkToken, making this cross-origin state change possible. Rationale: The advisory's kill chain hinges on a cross-site auto-POST that passes checkSecuredACL via the admin session cookie while skipping the CSRF token. Comparing Referer host to the served host isolates cross-origin state changes to the importer — a signal legitimate in-UI imports (same-origin Referer) will not produce. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f
ATT&CKT1189 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin following a bookmarked/external deep-link into the import UI
  • Browsers/extensions with strict referrer-policy stripping the Referer on legitimate same-site POSTs
  • Reverse-proxy or SSO rewrite that changes the Host seen in logs vs the Referer
  • API clients that don't send a Referer header at all
  • Federated/multi-domain wiki deployments where admin origin legitimately differs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the admin account (csUserName) and the off-origin RefHost — an unfamiliar external domain in Referer strongly implies a CSRF lure page. Correlate to any phishing email/chat delivered to that admin. 2) CONTAIN: reset the admin's credentials and revoke active YesWiki sessions; block the RefHost domain at the proxy. 3) HUNT: search the same host for a successful unserialize outcome — php process spawning a shell (UC3) and new web-shell/config writes (UC4) in the seconds after this request.

YesWiki web server (php-fpm/apache) spawning a shell — Doctrine RCE1 gadget outcome AIExploitation High
Detects the post-deserialization RCE outcome of CVE-2026-52777: a PHP or web-server process (php-fpm, apache2, httpd, nginx) spawning an interactive shell or recon binary, which is what a PHPGGC Doctrine/RCE1 chain (`system($cmd)` via __destruct) produces. Web servers legitimately almost never fork /bin/sh. Rationale: Article states the Doctrine gadget chains terminate in system($cmd) (RCE1); the web-server-parent → shell-child edge is the direct behavioural fingerprint of that outcome and is inherently rare for php-fpm/apache. Corroborated via PHPGGC docs confirming Doctrine RCE1 __destruct system() sink. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PHP application shelling out (e.g. ImageMagick/exec() for thumbnailing, git hooks, cron wrappers)
  • Deployment/CI scripts running as the web-server user invoking bash
  • Backup jobs launched by php-fpm calling tar/curl
  • Monitoring agents that exec whoami/id under the web user
  • Composer or artisan/console tasks spawning sub-shells during maintenance
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","gs ","ghostscript","composer","artisan","/usr/bin/git"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: capture the child process command line — an inline `sh -c` with recon (id/uname), a reverse-shell one-liner, or curl-to-pipe confirms exploitation; benign app exec() calls have predictable, app-specific arguments. Correlate the process time to a UC1 importer POST. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, and revoke the web-server service account's outbound access. 3) HUNT: enumerate files written by php-fpm since first hit (UC4), check for new cron/systemd persistence and outbound C2 from the web-server process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","php7.4","php8.0","php8.1","php8.2","php8.3","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","id","whoami","uname")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","python","perl","curl","wget")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PHP/web-server process writing a .php web shell or modifying wakka.config.php on YesWiki AIInstallation High
Detects the file-write RCE/persistence outcome of CVE-2026-52777: a php-fpm/apache/nginx process creating a new `.php` file (Doctrine/FW1 `file_put_contents($php_file,...)` gadget = dropped web shell) or modifying `wakka.config.php`. The advisory explicitly lists writing web shells and modifying wakka.config.php as post-exploit actions. Rationale: The advisory names FW1 (file_put_contents($php_file,$contents)) as a terminal gadget and explicitly cites writing web shells and modifying wakka.config.php as impact. A web-server process authoring new executable PHP outside cache dirs is a canonical web-shell drop; the config-file name is taken verbatim from the article. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-88xg-v53p-fpvf
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • YesWiki legitimately regenerating compiled/template PHP into cache directories (excluded by filter)
  • Administrator applying a YesWiki upgrade or plugin install that writes .php under the web root
  • Legitimate config change writing wakka.config.php during setup/reconfiguration
  • Composer/plugin installs run as the web-server user
  • Deployment automation syncing new .php files via the app service account
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer","artisan","upgrade","install"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: open the written file — short files with `eval`, `assert`, `system`, `base64_decode`, `$_POST`/`$_GET` passthrough, or `preg_replace /e` are web shells; compare wakka.config.php against the last known-good backup for injected handlers/credentials. 2) CONTAIN: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and rotate any secrets present in wakka.config.php and the MySQL DB it references. 3) HUNT: pivot on the writing process to find the triggering importer POST (UC1), check web logs for subsequent GET/POST access to the dropped filename, and scan sibling web roots on shared hosting for the same artifact.

PHP unserialize / object-injection errors in server logs — CVE-2026-52777 exploitation attempts AIExploitation Medium
Hunts PHP/web-server error logs for the deserialization fault signatures the article's PoC emits — `unserialize`, `Object of class ... could not be converted to string`, `__destruct`/`__wakeup` — which surface when gadget chains fire or fail (wrong dependency versions) against the BazarImport sink. Repeated occurrences in a short window indicate exploit iteration. Rationale: Taken directly from the PoC's verbatim output (`Object of class Gadget could not be converted to string`, `__destruct fired`) and the sink function `unserialize`. Failed or partial gadget chains against YesWiki's exact dependency graph will throw these, making the error log a low-cost tripwire for exploitation attempts even when the RCE itself fails. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate plugins/apps on the host that use unserialize and log benign warnings
  • Developers testing serialization code in staging that shares log pipelines
  • Log lines quoting these tokens in unrelated stack traces or security-scan noise
  • Other PHP apps on shared hosting emitting __wakeup/__destruct notices
  • Static-analysis or WAF products echoing 'PHP Object Injection' in their own log messages
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm the erroring script path is under tools/bazar (CSVManager.php importEntry) and the timestamp aligns with an importer POST (UC1); a burst of identical unserialize errors from one source implies exploit iteration. 2) CONTAIN: if tied to the importer, block the source IP, invalidate admin sessions, and verify the host is patched to YesWiki >= 4.6.6. 3) HUNT: even on 'failed' attempts, sweep the host for successful outcomes — web-server shell spawns (UC3) and new .php/config writes (UC4) — and confirm no gadget succeeded before dependency mismatch stopped later attempts.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "unserialize" or SyslogMessage has_all ("Object of class","could not be converted to string") or SyslogMessage has_any ("__destruct","__wakeup","PHP Object Injection")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki {{erasespamedcomments}} spam-cleanup action page planted via unauth write (CVE-2026-52766) AIDelivery High
Hunts the weaponization step of CVE-2026-52766 where an anonymous user abuses YesWiki's allow-by-default write ACL (default_write_acl='*') to POST a new wiki page whose body embeds the {{erasespamedcomments}} action. This action carries no authorization check, so planting it stages the subsequent arbitrary page-deletion trigger. Rationale: Pivots on the unique vulnerable action name 'erasespamedcomments' from actions/EraseSpamedCommentsAction.php combined with an HTTP POST — the string appears in no benign traffic, so any POST carrying it is either exploitation or authorized spam-cleanup. Cross-checked the YesWiki advisory history which shows the same allow-by-default ACL class (CVE-2025-46348). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6x7x-gcmf-7r8x • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wc9g-6j9w-hr95
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate wiki administrator creating or editing a real spam-cleanup page that embeds the {{erasespamedcomments}} action
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, Nuclei) probing the instance for CVE-2026-52766 after patch
  • Internal red-team or patch-validation testing of the fix in 4.6.6
  • WAF rule-testing traffic replaying the PoC request against a staging host
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP, User-Agent and session cookies for the POST; confirm whether the request carried an authenticated YesWiki admin cookie or was anonymous, and check the target wiki page name in the URL. 2) Contain: if anonymous, block the source IP at the WAF and immediately confirm the YesWiki version is < 4.6.6; if so, upgrade to 4.6.6 or restrict the 'erasespamedcomments' action ACL to admins in the permissions map. 3) Hunt: search the same source IP for a follow-on POST containing clean=yes + suppr[] (the deletion trigger) and review web/DB logs for DELETE activity against the pages/acls/tags tables.
CommonSecurityLog

| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL contains "erasespamedcomments" or RequestContext contains "erasespamedcomments" or Message contains "erasespamedcomments" or RequestCookies contains "erasespamedcomments"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki unauth arbitrary page deletion trigger — clean=yes + suppr[] POST (CVE-2026-52766) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exploitation/impact step of CVE-2026-52766: an anonymous POST submitting clean=yes together with the suppr[] array to a YesWiki page, which invokes PageManager::deleteOrphaned() and issues unconditional DELETEs against pages/links/acls/triples/referrers/tags. Flags deletion of the front page (PagePrincipale) as highest-impact. Rationale: Matches the exact PoC deletion form — the co-occurrence of clean=yes and the suppr[] array in a single POST is the specific EraseSpamedCommentsAction::run() delete branch and does not occur in normal page rendering. Targeting PagePrincipale surfaces front-page destruction, the article's stated worst-case impact. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6x7x-gcmf-7r8x • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wc9g-6j9w-hr95
ATT&CKT1485 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An authenticated administrator legitimately using the spam-cleanup feature to purge real spam comment pages
  • DAST/vuln-scanner (Nuclei, Burp) exercising the CVE-2026-52766 PoC against the instance
  • Patch-validation or red-team testing of the deletion path on a staging host
  • A WAF replaying the suppr[]/clean=yes signature during rule tuning
Suppression filter
and (RequestURL contains "PagePrincipale" or RequestContext contains "PagePrincipale" or Message contains "PagePrincipale")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source IP and whether the POST carried an authenticated admin session; enumerate the page tags in suppr[] (especially PagePrincipale, admin, or other users' pages) to gauge blast radius. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the wiki offline or enable hibernation if front/admin pages were deleted, and confirm/upgrade to YesWiki 4.6.6. 3) Hunt: pull DB/web logs to enumerate every deleted tag, restore pages/links/acls/tags rows from backup, and search the same IP for the preceding {{erasespamedcomments}} page-plant POST and for reconnaissance of other unauth actions.

Injective SDK on npm infected with cryptocurrency wallet stealer

BleepingComputerStepSecurity
2026-07-09 9 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 8, 2026, attackers used access to a trusted developer's account to slip a backdoor into a widely used software development kit for the Injective blockchain. Disguised as harmless analytics, the code quietly captured wallet recovery phrases and private keys and sent them to an attacker-controlled server the moment a wallet was created or loaded. Automatic publishing pushed the tainted code out to 18 related packages within minutes, and it stayed live for less than an hour before being pulled and fixed. If your application installed any of the affected packages during that window, or pic…

Exfil beacon to fake Injective gRPC-Web domain (testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network) AICommand & Control High
Hunts host/process resolution of or connection to the exact attacker exfiltration FQDN used by the backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 payload, which base64-encodes wallet mnemonics/private keys and POSTs them there while masquerading as legitimate Injective gRPC-Web infrastructure. This is the single highest-fidelity IOC in the campaign and fires the moment PrivateKey.fromMnemonic/fromHex leaks a secret. Rationale: Uses the exact exfil FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network confirmed by StepSecurity/Socket as the HTTPS POST endpoint; the string is a crafted look-alike that is NOT a real Injective endpoint, so any resolution is malicious with near-zero base rate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/injective-npm-supply-chain-attack-18-packages-backdoored-to-steal-crypto-wallet-keys • https://crypto.news/compromised-injective-sdk-sends-wallet-keys-through-fake-telemetry/ • https://cointelegraph.com/news/hackers-compromise-injective-npm-package-with-malware-to-steal-wallet-keys
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / malware sandbox intentionally detonating sdk-ts@1.20.21 to study it
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving the IOC domain for validation
  • An analyst pasting the FQDN into a browser or curl during triage
  • DNS sinkhole / RPZ appliance logging the block itself as a resolution event
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("threatconnect","virustotal"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName (expect node.exe or an Electron/browser wallet app) and the developer/build host; pull the loaded @injectivelabs package versions from that host's node_modules. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy, isolate the host, and treat every wallet seed phrase / private key that host handled since first install as compromised — force key rotation and fund migration for affected wallets. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for resolution of the same FQDN and for the key-derivation-telemetry payload file, and pivot on the initiating process across the fleet.

Malicious npm payload file key-derivation-telemetry.(js|ts) dropped under node_modules/@injectivelabs AIInstallation High
Detects the file-system artifact unique to the backdoored SDK — a 79-line helper named key-derivation-telemetry.ts/.js that wires trackKeyDerivation() into PrivateKey.fromMnemonic/fromHex. This file exists only in the compromised 1.20.21 release of @injectivelabs/sdk-ts and never in a clean install, making the filename+path a definitive supply-chain indicator. Rationale: The filename key-derivation-telemetry.ts/.js is the exact payload artifact named in the article and is absent from clean SDK releases; scoping to the @injectivelabs path removes any coincidental same-named files elsewhere. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/injective-npm-supply-chain-attack-18-packages-backdoored-to-steal-crypto-wallet-keys • https://socket.dev/blog
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer who cloned the compromised commit for analysis/repro purposes
  • Backup/restore or file-sync software re-writing an old cached node_modules containing the artifact
  • Malware-analysis sandbox extracting the package tarball
  • EDR/AV quarantine relocation events referencing the payload path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","tar.exe","7z.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is a package manager (node.exe/npm/pnpm/yarn) and record the exact @injectivelabs package + version from the FolderPath. 2) Contain: quarantine node_modules on the host, purge npm/pnpm/yarn caches (the article warns cached copies persist), and rebuild from a clean lockfile pinned to >=1.20.23. 3) Hunt: correlate the host to any resolution of the exfil FQDN (UC1) to confirm whether secrets were actually leaked, and enumerate downstream apps that bundled this build.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("key-derivation-telemetry.js","key-derivation-telemetry.ts")
| where FolderPath has "@injectivelabs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("key-derivation-telemetry.js","key-derivation-telemetry.ts")
| where TargetFilePath has "@injectivelabs"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Install/pin of backdoored @injectivelabs packages at malicious version 1.20.21 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts package-manager process invocations that explicitly reference the compromised @injectivelabs release 1.20.21 across the SDK and its 17 transitively-pinned sibling packages. The clean re-release is 1.20.23, so any explicit 1.20.21 install string indicates a host that pulled the backdoored train. Rationale: 1.20.21 is the exact malicious version named for all 18 @injectivelabs packages (Socket/StepSecurity), and it was superseded by the clean 1.20.23 — an explicit 1.20.21 install string is a precise supply-chain tell with negligible legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/injective-npm-supply-chain-attack-18-packages-backdoored-to-steal-crypto-wallet-keys • https://cointelegraph.com/news/hackers-compromise-injective-npm-package-with-malware-to-steal-wallet-keys
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR/security engineer deliberately reproducing the compromised install to study the payload
  • A `npm view`/`npm audit` or SCA scanner emitting the version string on the command line during remediation checks
  • Internal advisory automation that references 1.20.21 as a blocked version in its invocation
  • A developer copy-pasting the vulnerable version from a writeup before correcting to 1.20.23
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually resolved/installed (vs merely referenced) 1.20.21 by checking for the payload file (UC2) and node_modules/@injectivelabs/*/package.json version. 2) Contain: pin all @injectivelabs dependencies to >=1.20.23, wipe and rebuild node_modules, and clear the package-manager cache to evict the poisoned tarball. 3) Hunt: pivot to any wallet-handling application that took this build as a dependency and check those hosts for exfil-domain resolution; rotate any keys those apps touched.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","pnpm.exe","pnpm.cmd","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@injectivelabs" and ProcessCommandLine has "1.20.21"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "@injectivelabs" and CommandLine has "1.20.21"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New GigaWiper Windows Backdoor Bundles Disk Wiping, Fake Ransomware, and Spyware

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 15 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft has taken apart a destructive Windows backdoor it calls GigaWiper. What stands out is how it is built: not one tool but three older destructive programs bolted into one, offered as commands the operator can choose from. Each is a different way to break a machine: wipe the whole disk, overwrite the Windows drive, or run fake "ransomware" that scrambles files with a key it never saves

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — New GigaWiper Windows Backdoor Bundles Disk Wiping, Fake Ransomware, and Spyware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GigaWiper 'OneDrive Update' scheduled task firing every minute · [LLM] GigaWiper self-tracking registry key HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GigaWiper firewall rule masquerading as Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost · [LLM] GigaWiper C2 over RabbitMQ/Redis/MinIO or known command servers from endpoints · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] takeown/icacls seizing ownership of Windows boot files (bootmgr, ntoskrnl.exe) · [LLM] GigaWiper fake ransomware: mass '.candy' file writes and wallpaper swap · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
GigaWiper 'OneDrive Update' scheduled task firing every minute AIInstallation High
Hunts GigaWiper/BLUERABBIT persistence: a scheduled task masquerading as 'OneDrive Update' created with a one-minute repeat interval via schtasks.exe. Legitimate OneDrive updater tasks never run every minute, making the minute cadence the high-fidelity tell. Rationale: Uses the article's exact task name 'OneDrive Update' plus the one-minute (/sc minute /mo 1) trigger, which is the differentiator from Microsoft's legit OneDrive updater tasks. Corroborated by Binary Defense's BLUERABBIT write-up describing the same persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-bluerabbit-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise RMM/GPO deploying a genuinely-named OneDrive maintenance task (rare, and not at 1-minute cadence)
  • Admin manually testing schtasks with a 'OneDrive' string in a lab
  • Software packaging tools (PDQ, SCCM) creating high-frequency check-in tasks that coincidentally reference OneDrive
  • Third-party backup agents that re-register OneDrive sync tasks
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft OneDrive"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full schtasks command line and the task XML (schtasks /query /tn "OneDrive Update" /xml); confirm the action points to a non-Microsoft binary outside %ProgramFiles%\Microsoft OneDrive. 2) Contain: disable/delete the task, isolate the host in Defender, and snapshot memory before reboot (wiper may trigger on reboot). 3) Hunt: pivot on the task's action binary hash across the fleet, check HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment (UC2) and the Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost firewall rule (UC3) on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "OneDrive Update"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("minute", "/mo 1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "OneDrive Update"
| where CommandLine has_any ("minute", "/mo 1")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: GigaWiper OneDrive Update Scheduled Task Every Minute
id: 3f2b9c14-8a71-4d0e-9c2a-5b7e1f0a9d34
description: Detects creation of a scheduled task masquerading as 'OneDrive Update' with a one-minute repeat interval, matching GigaWiper/BLUERABBIT persistence.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-gigawiper-windows-backdoor-bundles.html
  - https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'OneDrive Update'
      - 'minute'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE OR *\\Schtasks.exe) @CommandLine:*OneDrive*Update* @CommandLine:(*minute* OR *MINUTE* OR *Minute*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i CommandLine=/OneDrive Update/i CommandLine=/minute/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe Processes.process="*OneDrive Update*" (Processes.process="*minute*" OR Processes.process="*/mo 1*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe Processes.process="*OneDrive Update*" (Processes.process="*minute*" OR Processes.process="*/mo 1*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
GigaWiper self-tracking registry key HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment AIInstallation High
Hunts the GigaWiper masquerade artifact: a value written under HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment (note: NOT the legitimate HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive path) used by the implant to track itself while posing as OneDrive. Rationale: Uses the exact article-named key HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment and explicitly excludes the real HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive path, so the only hits are the implant's masquerade. Falcon FDR AsepValueUpdate only covers autostart keys, so this non-ASEP key is left empty for LogScale. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities • https://gbhackers.com/bluerabbit-backdoor-encrypts-files/
ATT&CKT1112 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party tool coincidentally creating an 'OneDrive\Environment' subkey (uncommon)
  • Backup/migration tooling cloning HKCU hives between profiles
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in an instrumented VM
  • Manual regedit exploration during IR of an already-known host
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the value data under the key and the InitiatingProcess that wrote it; the writing process is the implant. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve the process binary (hash it against the four GigaWiper SHA256s) before any reboot to avoid triggering the wiper. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same key and cross-reference hosts also showing the 'OneDrive Update' minute task (UC1) and outbound RabbitMQ/Redis/MinIO to the C2 IPs (UC5).
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"OneDrive\Environment"
| where RegistryKey !has @"Microsoft\OneDrive"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "onedrive.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"OneDrive\Environment"
| where RegistryKey !has @"Microsoft\OneDrive"
| where ActingProcessName !has "onedrive.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

GigaWiper firewall rule masquerading as Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost AICommand & Control High
Hunts GigaWiper opening its remote-control (hidden VNC) channel by adding an inbound Windows Firewall rule named after a real component, Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost, via netsh advfirewall or New-NetFirewallRule. Rationale: Uses the exact firewall-rule masquerade name Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost from the article; that real component never legitimately requires an operator-added inbound netsh/PowerShell firewall rule, making command-line references high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-gigawiper-windows-backdoor-bundles.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-bluerabbit-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1562.004 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint management tooling scripting firewall rules that reference CloudExperienceHost by coincidence (very rare)
  • IT admin troubleshooting OOBE/CloudExperienceHost connectivity manually
  • Security baseline/GPO hardening scripts touching CloudExperienceHost
  • Custom imaging scripts adding named firewall exceptions
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate the new firewall rule (netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name=Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost) and identify the local port it opens and the binary bound to it. 2) Contain: delete the rule, block inbound at network layer, and isolate the host; the rule fronts a VNC/remote-control channel. 3) Hunt: look for listening sockets and inbound connections from the C2 IPs 185.182.193.21 / 212.8.248.104, plus co-occurring UC1/UC2 artifacts on the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "CloudExperienceHost"
| where (FileName =~ "netsh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "advfirewall" and ProcessCommandLine has "add")
     or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "New-NetFirewallRule")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "CloudExperienceHost"
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\netsh.exe" and CommandLine has "advfirewall" and CommandLine has "add")
     or (NewProcessName has "powershell" and CommandLine has "New-NetFirewallRule")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

takeown/icacls seizing ownership of Windows boot files (bootmgr, ntoskrnl.exe) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the GigaWiper pre-destruction step: takeown.exe and icacls.exe used to seize ownership/ACLs of boot-critical files such as bootmgr and ntoskrnl.exe, a strong precursor to the raw-disk/Windows-drive wipers. Rationale: Directly implements the article's stated defender signal: takeown/icacls taking ownership of bootmgr and ntoskrnl.exe outside maintenance windows. Ownership seizure of boot files by these LOLBins is almost never legitimate on endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-gigawiper-windows-backdoor-bundles.html • https://gbhackers.com/bluerabbit-backdoor-encrypts-files/
ATT&CKT1222.001 T1561.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate boot-repair (bcdedit/DISM/sfc) sessions during OS servicing where an admin scripts takeown on boot files
  • Dual-boot or imaging engineers adjusting boot-file ACLs
  • In-place Windows feature-update rollback touching bootmgr
  • Forensic tooling normalizing permissions on a mounted image
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("trustedinstaller.exe","dism.exe","tiworker.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm this is outside a change/maintenance window and identify the initiating process/user; boot-file ownership changes on a workstation are almost always malicious. 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host and do NOT reboot (wipers commonly trigger on reboot); capture a disk/memory image. 3) Hunt: search the same host and peers for raw disk-write handles (\\.\PhysicalDrive), event-log clearing (wevtutil cl), and the C2 IPs; treat any host with this signal as pre-detonation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("takeown.exe","icacls.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bootmgr","ntoskrnl.exe","bootmgfw")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\takeown.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\icacls.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("bootmgr","ntoskrnl.exe","bootmgfw")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: takeown/icacls on Windows Boot Files as Wiper Precursor
id: e4a0c8b3-71f2-4d6a-9b15-3c8e0d2a7f19
description: Detects takeown.exe or icacls.exe operating on boot-critical files (bootmgr, ntoskrnl.exe, bootmgfw), a GigaWiper pre-wipe step to remove protections before disk destruction.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-gigawiper-windows-backdoor-bundles.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:

  - attack.t1561.002

      - '\icacls.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'bootmgr'
      - 'ntoskrnl.exe'
      - 'bootmgfw'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\takeown.exe OR *\\TAKEOWN.EXE OR *\\icacls.exe OR *\\ICACLS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*bootmgr* OR *ntoskrnl.exe* OR *ntoskrnl.EXE* OR *bootmgfw*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(takeown|icacls)\.exe$/i CommandLine=/(bootmgr|ntoskrnl\.exe|bootmgfw)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN (takeown.exe,icacls.exe) (Processes.process="*bootmgr*" OR Processes.process="*ntoskrnl.exe*" OR Processes.process="*bootmgfw*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN (takeown.exe,icacls.exe) (Processes.process="*bootmgr*" OR Processes.process="*ntoskrnl.exe*" OR Processes.process="*bootmgfw*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
GigaWiper C2 over RabbitMQ/Redis/MinIO or known command servers from endpoints AICommand & Control High
Hunts GigaWiper command traffic that rides legitimate services (RabbitMQ 5672 tasking, Redis 6379 results, MinIO 9000 exfil) to public IPs, or any connection to the two named command servers 185.182.193.21 and 212.8.248.104. Rationale: Combines the two article/vendor-confirmed C2 IPs (high-fidelity, any port) with the RabbitMQ/Redis/MinIO port set restricted to public destinations, matching the article's 'RabbitMQ or Redis traffic from ordinary desktops rather than servers.' IPs corroborated by Binary Defense (same command servers as BLUERABBIT). Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-bluerabbit-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1071 T1567 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/DevOps workstations legitimately connecting to a cloud-hosted RabbitMQ/Redis/MinIO (5672/6379/9000) over the internet
  • Managed message-broker SaaS (CloudAMQP, Redis Enterprise Cloud, self-hosted MinIO on a public VPS)
  • CI runners on desktops pulling artifacts from a public MinIO bucket
  • Monitoring agents polling a public Redis endpoint
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\\Users\\", @"\\Windows\\Temp\\", @"\\AppData\\") or RemoteIP in ("185.182.193.21","212.8.248.104")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process; a broker/store client (or a Go binary in a temp/user path) on a non-server desktop reaching these ports/IPs is suspicious. Connections to 185.182.193.21/212.8.248.104 are alert-worthy regardless of port. 2) Contain: block both C2 IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, and preserve state before reboot. 3) Hunt: enumerate all internal hosts touching those IPs/ports, correlate with UC1–UC4 host artifacts, and check MinIO (9000) sessions for outbound exfil volume.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("185.182.193.21","212.8.248.104")
     or (RemotePort in (5672,6379,9000) and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("185.182.193.21","212.8.248.104")
     or (DstPortNumber in (5672,6379,9000) and DstIpAddr !startswith "10." and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber) by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: GigaWiper Connection to Known Command Servers

GigaWiper fake ransomware: mass '.candy' file writes and wallpaper swap AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Crucio-derived fake-ransomware module: bulk creation/rename of files with the .candy extension on a single host (no ransom note, no recoverable key), optionally paired with a desktop wallpaper change to an alarming warning image. Rationale: Uses the article's exact .candy extension left by the Crucio-based fake-ransomware module, with a per-host volume threshold (>=25) to separate a mass-encryption event from an isolated filename. Corroborated by Binary Defense/BLUERABBIT reporting the same encrypt-then-wipe behavior. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-bluerabbit-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1486 T1491.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche application legitimately using a .candy file extension for its own data (rare)
  • Malware researcher replaying the sample in a sandbox
  • Backup software creating many files that a naming scheme coincidentally suffixes with .candy
  • A single user renaming a handful of files (filtered by the >=25 threshold)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess writing .candy files and its hash; because the key is never saved, treat this as destruction, not recoverable ransomware. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, kill the process, and pull it offline before it pivots to the disk/Windows-drive wipers; preserve a forensic image. 3) Hunt: check the host for wallpaper changes (HKCU\Control Panel\Desktop\Wallpaper), event-log clearing, and the boot-file takeown/icacls (UC4); sweep peers for the four GigaWiper SHA256 hashes and the C2 IPs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName endswith ".candy"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), FileCount=dcount(FolderPath), SamplePath=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| where FileCount >= 25
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".candy"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), FileCount=dcount(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| where FileCount >= 25
| order by FirstSeen desc

                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd") or SHA1 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd") or MD5 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd") or SHA1 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd") or MD5 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] UAT-7810 ORB network C2 beaconing to known LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH relay IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
UAT-7810 ORB network C2 beaconing to known LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH relay IPs AICommand & Control High
Hunts internal hosts establishing outbound connections to the four command-and-control server IPs Talos attributed to the China-nexus UAT-7810 ORB campaign. Because these are hard IOCs for the actor's intermediate C2 relays, any egress to them from managed endpoints is high-fidelity evidence of LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH backend communication. Rationale: Uses the four hard C2 IPs (194.233.92.26, 217.15.160.247, 217.15.164.147, 95.182.100.231) Talos published for the UAT-7810 ORB relays — corroborated by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News write-ups of the same report. Any egress to these is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/china-linked-uat-7810-expands-orb.html
ATT&CKT1571 T1090.003 T1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/VirusTotal detonation sandbox hosts deliberately reaching the IPs
  • Security researcher or IR team validating IOCs from a jump box
  • Shared-hosting IP later re-provisioned to a benign tenant after Talos publication
  • Corporate proxy/NAT egress IP appearing as SourceIP masking the true internal host
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonate","malware-lab") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal DeviceName/src_host and the initiating process; confirm the connection was outbound and not a scanner hitting your perimeter. Check whether the host is an edge/router-adjacent system. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block all four IPs at the firewall/proxy, and preserve the process binary + memory for LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH triage. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process hash across the fleet, review any Ruckus/ASUS routers on the same segment for CVE-2023-25717 / CVE-2025-2492 exploitation, and check for multi-protocol proxy behaviour (DNS/SOCKS/ICMP tunnels) characteristic of LONGLEASH.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort), Procs=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort) by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by LastSeen desc
