Exposed Ruckus/ASUS routers vulnerable to UAT-7810 n-day exploitation (CVE-2023-25717, CVE-2025-2492) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces managed devices whose vulnerability inventory shows the specific Ruckus and ASUS router n-days UAT-7810 exploits for ORB initial access. This is a proactive exposure hunt: the actor relies exclusively on these unpatched edge-device CVEs, so any device carrying them is a prioritised patch/monitor target. Rationale: Uses the exact four CVEs Talos named as UAT-7810's initial-access vector — CVE-2023-25717 and CVE-2020-22653/22658 (Ruckus) plus CVE-2025-2492 (ASUS AiCloud auth bypass, CVSS 9.2, confirmed via NVD). Exposure-first hunt because the actor uses no other entry method. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-2492 • https://thehackernews.com/2025/04/asus-confirms-critical-flaw-in-aicloud.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Router already patched but TVM inventory stale before next scan cycle
  • Non-internet-facing lab/test router carrying the CVE but not exposed
  • Vendor-labelled software version overlapping a fixed build (version-range false match)
  • Device decommissioned but still in the asset inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device is a real Ruckus/ASUS router (not a false software match) and determine internet exposure via DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing. 2) Contain: prioritise firmware patching for internet-facing units; where patching is delayed, restrict management-interface (AiCloud/WebUI) access to trusted admin subnets and enforce MFA. 3) Hunt: cross-reference these device IPs against the UAT-7810 C2-beacon detection, review router auth/management logs for unauthenticated access consistent with CVE-2025-2492, and check for unexpected outbound proxy sessions indicating ORB enrolment.

| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

New Helix vishing group emerges in SharePoint data theft attacks

BleepingComputer
2026-07-09 9 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new data-extortion group called Helix is using identity-focused tactics such as voice phishing (vishing), device code phishing, and multi-factor authentication (MFA) abuse to steal data from SharePoint environments. [...]

IPs179.43.185.230 179.43.185.226 179.43.171.42

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Endpoint contact to Helix device-code phishing domain oskeysync.com · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Entra ID device-code authentication success (Helix vishing entry vector) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] New MFA method registered within 2h of a device-code sign-in (Helix persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Automated SharePoint enumeration via python-requests/2.28.1 from Helix IP · [LLM] Bulk SharePoint download spike from Helix python-requests client
Entra ID device-code authentication success (Helix vishing entry vector) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins completed via the device-code OAuth flow, the mechanism Helix operators trick vished employees into approving to capture session tokens without a password. Device-code auth is rare in most tenants and is the single control ReliaQuest recommends disabling, so successful device-code sign-ins warrant per-user review. Rationale: Anchors on the device-code auth flow that ReliaQuest names as Helix's defining entry vector and the highest-value control to disable; uses AuthenticationProcessingDetails 'Device Code' marker (schema-present) rather than raw IOC so it survives infrastructure rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-helix-extortion-group/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/helix-data-extortion-group-uses-vishing-and-device-code-phishing/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/blackfile-vishing-extortion-operation
ATT&CKT1528 T1078.004 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running `az login --use-device-code` or `Connect-AzAccount -UseDeviceAuthentication`
  • Teams Rooms / conference-room devices and smart TVs provisioning via device code
  • IoT and shared-kiosk device onboarding
  • Legitimate PowerShell/Graph automation using device-code grant
  • Users on locked-down VDI where browser SSO fails and they fall back to device code
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Microsoft Authentication Broker")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the user's recent sign-ins — is device-code auth normal for them? Check IPAddress/ASN and City vs their usual location and whether the app is Azure CLI/PowerShell (benign) vs a resource app like SharePoint/Graph (suspicious). Cross-reference any help-desk report of a vishing call. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), disable device-code flow via Conditional Access, and force credential + MFA re-registration review. 3) HUNT: Check AuditLogs for a new MFA method registered by this user in the next 2h (UC2) and OfficeActivity for python-requests SharePoint access from the same identity (UC3/UC4).
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where isnotempty(AccountUpn) and AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), Cities=make_set(City,5), Apps=make_set(Application,5) by AccountUpn, Country
| order by FirstSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| extend City = tostring(LocationDetails.city)

New MFA method registered within 2h of a device-code sign-in (Helix persistence) AIInstallation High
Correlates a successful device-code Entra sign-in with a new security-info / MFA authenticator registration by the same identity inside a 2-hour window. Helix operators 'quickly register a new multi-factor authenticator app for persistence' immediately after gaining token access, so this pairing is a high-fidelity account-takeover-to-persistence signal. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit sequence (device-code access → immediate new MFA authenticator registration) as a temporal correlation, which is far higher fidelity than either event alone and resistant to IOC rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-helix-extortion-group/ • https://www.cryptika.com/helix-data-extortion-group-uses-vishing-and-device-code-phishing-to-steal-sharepoint-data/

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Change.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • New-hire onboarding where first sign-in and MFA enrollment legitimately happen together
  • User replacing a lost/reset phone and re-enrolling an authenticator
  • IT-assisted MFA reset following a legitimate help-desk ticket
  • Bulk MFA re-registration campaign after a policy change
  • Self-service password reset flows that also touch security info

| where OperationName !has "Admin" | where TargetUpn !in (dynamic(["onboarding-svc@contoso.com"]))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the device-code sign-in IP/geo is anomalous for the user and check whether a help-desk ticket or onboarding record explains the MFA change. Inspect which authenticator (app vs phone) was added and from what device. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, delete the newly registered MFA method, revoke sessions (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), and reset credentials. 3) HUNT: Pivot to OfficeActivity for the same UserId hitting SharePoint with a python-requests user-agent or from 179.43.185.230/226 (UC3/UC4), and review all content the identity accessed to scope exfiltration.

Automated SharePoint enumeration via python-requests/2.28.1 from Helix IP AIActions on Objectives High
Detects scripted SharePoint access using the python-requests/2.28.1 user-agent and/or originating from Helix exfil hosts 179.43.185.230 and 179.43.185.226 (AS 51852, Private Layer INC), including the contentclass:STS_Site and wildcard search enumeration ReliaQuest calls Helix's most reliable fingerprint. Interactive users never carry a python-requests agent, making this a very high-signal indicator of automated tenant inventory. Rationale: Combines three corroborated Helix fingerprints — the exact python-requests/2.28.1 user-agent, the AS 51852 exfil IPs, and the contentclass:STS_Site search string — each of which is anomalous for interactive M365 usage; ReliaQuest explicitly names this the most reliable cross-incident fingerprint. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-helix-extortion-group/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/helix-data-extortion-group-uses-vishing-and-device-code-phishing/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/blackfile-vishing-extortion-operation
ATT&CKT1213.002 T1083
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned SharePoint migration tooling (AvePoint, Metalogix/Quest) using script agents
  • Internal Python/Graph automation or reporting jobs with a python-requests agent
  • eDiscovery / compliance content search exports
  • Backup vendors (Veeam for M365, Barracuda) enumerating sites
  • Approved RPA bots inventorying document libraries
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !in~ ("svc-sharepoint-backup","avepoint-migration") and IPAddress in ("179.43.185.230","179.43.185.226") or (UserAgent has "python-requests" and AccountDisplayName !in~ ("svc-sharepoint-backup","avepoint-migration"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether the python-requests agent / ClientIP maps to a sanctioned automation account. Any hit from 179.43.185.230 or 179.43.185.226 is a confirmed Helix IOC — treat as true positive. Review the search operations and count of sites touched. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the identity's sessions and refresh tokens, block the source IPs at the CASB/conditional-access network layer, and disable the account pending review. 3) HUNT: Immediately pivot to FileDownloaded volume for the same session (UC4), enumerate exactly which sites/files were returned to scope the breach, and check for the preceding device-code sign-in and MFA registration (UC1/UC2).

| where Application has "SharePoint"
| where UserAgent has "python-requests" or IPAddress in ("179.43.185.230","179.43.185.226")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Actions=make_set(ActionType,25), ActionCount=count(), Objects=dcount(ObjectName) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, UserAgent, ISP
| order by ActionCount desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OfficeWorkload has "SharePoint"
| where UserAgent has "python-requests" or ClientIP in ("179.43.185.230","179.43.185.226") or Parameters has "contentclass:STS_Site"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Ops=make_set(Operation,25), OpCount=count(), Sites=dcount(Site_Url) by UserId, ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by OpCount desc
CLOUD
index=o365 sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Workload=SharePoint
| search UserAgent="python-requests/2.28.1" OR UserAgent="python-requests*" OR ClientIP IN ("179.43.185.230","179.43.185.226") OR _raw="*contentclass:STS_Site*"
| stats earliest(_time) as firstSeen latest(_time) as lastSeen count values(Operation) as ops dc(Site_Url) as sites by UserId, ClientIP, UserAgent
| sort - count
Bulk SharePoint download spike from Helix python-requests client AIActions on Objectives High
Detects high-volume automated SharePoint/OneDrive file downloads within a single hour tied to the python-requests user-agent or the Helix exfil IPs 179.43.185.230/226 — the bulk-collection stage that follows Helix enumeration. A scripted client pulling dozens-to-hundreds of files per hour is the collection/exfiltration behaviour ReliaQuest observed executing from the same host and agent as the enumeration. Rationale: Targets the collection/exfil stage by pairing the python-requests agent and AS 51852 IOC IPs with a per-hour download-volume threshold (>50), catching the scripted bulk pull ReliaQuest observed from the same host/agent as enumeration. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-helix-extortion-group/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/helix-data-extortion-group-uses-vishing-and-device-code-phishing/

Data sources

| where AccountDisplayName !in~ ("svc-m365-backup","veeam-o365","avepoint-migration")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Any hit from 179.43.185.230/226 is a confirmed Helix IOC — escalate. Otherwise confirm the python-requests agent isn't a sanctioned backup/sync account and review the distinct-file count and site scope. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the identity's tokens, block the source IPs, disable the account, and preserve the OfficeActivity records for scoping. 3) HUNT: Reconstruct the exact file list downloaded to size the data-theft, check whether the same identity earlier ran the contentclass:STS_Site enumeration (UC3), and watch for follow-on extortion contact.

OfficeActivity

APPLICATION
index=o365 sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Workload=SharePoint Operation IN ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileAccessed")

Endpoint contact to Helix device-code phishing domain oskeysync.com AIDelivery High
Detects DNS/web resolution of oskeysync.com and its target-specific subdomains — the NICENIC-registered domain Helix uses to host device-code phishing pages during vishing calls. A managed endpoint resolving this domain indicates a victim was steered to the Helix credential-capture page. Rationale: oskeysync.com is a corroborated Helix IOC (BleepingComputer + Cryptika/ReliaQuest) registered via NICENIC — the same registrar tied to ShinyHunters; `has`/endswith matching catches the target-specific subdomains ReliaQuest reported under it. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cryptika.com/helix-data-extortion-group-uses-vishing-and-device-code-phishing-to-steal-sharepoint-data/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-helix-extortion-group/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1528
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-team detonation of the IOC in a sandbox or threat-intel validation
  • Automated threat-intel feed resolvers pre-resolving indicator domains
  • Web proxy/secure-gateway pre-fetch of a blocked URL
  • Researcher browsing the phishing page for analysis
  • Unrelated typosquat resolution by a curious user who did not authenticate
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the user/host that resolved oskeysync.com and the initiating process (browser vs tooling); check for a concurrent vishing/help-desk report and whether a device-code sign-in for that user followed shortly after. 2) CONTAIN: Sink-hole/block oskeysync.com and all subdomains at DNS/proxy, isolate the host if a browser initiated it, and pre-emptively revoke the user's sessions. 3) HUNT: Correlate to a device-code sign-in (UC1) and new MFA registration (UC2) for the same user within the following hours, and sweep all endpoints for other resolutions of the domain or its subdomains.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteUrl has "oskeysync.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "oskeysync.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

npm 12 Disables Install Scripts by Default to Reduce Supply Chain Risk

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 6 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

GitHub has officially announced the release of npm version 12 with install scripts disabled by default, along with deprecating granular access tokens (GATs) designed to bypass two-factor authentication (2FA). The Microsoft-owned subsidiary noted that the following npm install behaviors that used to run automatically before have been made opt-in&nbsp;- allowScripts defaults to off, meaning

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Compromised @injectivelabs/sdk-ts exfiltrates wallet keys through fake telemetry

Aikido
2026-07-09 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious release of @injectivelabs/sdk-ts hid a wallet-key stealer inside code labeled as usage telemetry, then spread it across 17 more npm packages. Here's how it worked and how to check your projects. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1555.003
Domainstestnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network
SHA256103c4e6181151c1b… 9a59eb454f3ca3fe…

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Compromised @injectivelabs/sdk-ts exfiltrates wallet keys through fake telemetry
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound DNS/network activity to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network, the character-code-rebuilt exfil host used by the trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 to smuggle base64 wallet key material inside an X-Request-Id header disguised as gRPC-web traffic. Article-specific because the FQDN is a fixed IOC unique to this campaign. Rationale: The exfil FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network is a fixed, campaign-unique IOC (a lookalike subdomain never served by real Injective infra); matching it exactly avoids the FP risk of the parent injective.network.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1132.001 T1041 T1001.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate future Injective testnet archival endpoint being stood up under this exact FQDN (verify DNS/PKI ownership)
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonating the malicious package intentionally
  • Threat-intel sinkhole or research VM deliberately resolving the IOC
  • Internal DNS logging replaying old cached queries
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving host ran an @injectivelabs-dependent app; capture the initiating process (node.exe) and user. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat every wallet mnemonic/private key derived on it as exposed — freeze/rotate. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts querying the FQDN, pull package-lock/yarn.lock for @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21, and search DeviceFileEvents for the two malicious build artifacts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk AIInstallation Medium
Detects the two poisoned build files (accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) from @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 landing on disk, matched on their exact SHA-256 hashes. High fidelity IOC match that survives file renaming. Rationale: Both SHA-256 values are published IOCs for the exact malicious build artifacts; a hash match is unambiguous and near-zero FP, catching the stealer even if the file is renamed during transitive install.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / malware analyst intentionally storing the sample
  • Backup or EDR quarantine copy of the artifact triggering a second file event
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion writing the IOC file to a sandbox share
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and host; confirm whether it is a dev/CI machine or an analyst sandbox. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the affected node_modules, and pin @injectivelabs/* to a clean version (>=1.20.23); treat any wallet keys handled on the host as compromised. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints/CI runners for the same hashes and for outbound contact to the exfil FQDN.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Structural supply-chain detection: the campaign-unique build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js appearing under a node_modules/@injectivelabs path. Resilient to re-signing/re-hash because it keys on the version-marker filenames + package scope rather than the SHA-256, catching victims who pulled the stealer transitively via any of the 18 sibling packages. Rationale: The build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js are unique to the poisoned 1.20.21 dist and act as a version marker; combined with the node_modules/@injectivelabs scope this flags transitive victims (e.g. via wallet-core) who never named sdk-ts directly, and survives re-hash of the still-downloadable deprecated package.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Aikido/other scanner replaying the artifact during a rescan
  • Developer intentionally checking out the compromised version to reproduce/analyze
  • A future clean @injectivelabs build coincidentally reusing the same hashed chunk name (unlikely — Rollup chunk hashes are content-derived)
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each hit, read the package's package.json version and lockfile to confirm 1.20.21 was resolved (directly or transitively). 2) Contain: delete node_modules, repin @injectivelabs/* to >=1.20.23, and rebuild; flag any wallet keys/seed phrases derived on the host for rotation. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo/CI job with @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21 in lockfiles and correlate hosts against exfil-domain contacts and the SHA-256 file detection.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where FolderPath contains "node_modules" and FolderPath contains "injectivelabs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where TargetFilePath contains "node_modules" and TargetFilePath contains "injectivelabs"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ThreatsDay: Cloud Bucket Hijacking, Windows LPE Chain, Global Fraud Bust + 17 More Stories

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 24 use cases 12 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Most security mess starts as admin work. A link gets clicked. A tool gets trusted. A bucket name gets reused. A setting stays loose because nobody wants to touch&nbsp;it. This week is full of that kind of damage. Not loud. Not clever. Just small gaps doing big jobs. The worst part is how normal it all looks until the bill arrives. The full ThreatsDay list is below. Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] EtherRAT delivery: cmd.exe → curl.exe fetching v7.msi from camorreado.click · [LLM] Teams-lure RMM install: HopToDesk + AnyDesk launched from Teams/browser · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Esri ArcGIS Server CVE-2026-9181 path traversal in REST Uploads resource · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: Cloud Bucket Hijacking, Windows LPE Chain, Global Fraud Bust + 17 Mo
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] EtherRAT loader: msiexec runs v7.msi then node.exe executes staged JS runtime · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Payment-SDK typosquat exfil: node/python egress to *.ngrok-free.dev from build host · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
EtherRAT delivery: cmd.exe → curl.exe fetching v7.msi from camorreado.click AIDelivery High
Hunts the Unit 42 EtherRAT delivery step where a fake Teams 'System Administrator' guides the victim to run cmd.exe which shells out to curl.exe to download a malicious MSI (v7.msi, one of v1–v9) from camorreado[.]click. Anchored on the specific staging domain and the curl-downloads-MSI chain. Rationale: camorreado[.]click and v7.msi are named in the article and confirmed by BleepingComputer/gbhackers write-ups of the same Unit 42 EtherRAT campaign; curl.exe fetching an MSI from that domain is a single high-fidelity chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-it-support-calls-on-microsoft-teams-push-etherrat-malware/ • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-abuse-cross-tenant-teams-chat/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.003 T1204.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin using curl in cmd to pull a legit vendor MSI over HTTP
  • Software packaging/CI scripts that fetch MSIs via curl
  • Chocolatey/winget wrappers shelling out to curl
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chocolatey","winget","packer") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full curl command line and confirm the URL is camorreado[.]click or another vX.msi path; capture the downloaded MSI hash and the parent cmd/Teams context. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block camorreado[.]click at proxy/DNS, kill msiexec/node child processes, and revoke the user's active sessions. 3) Hunt: search the estate for HopToDesk.exe/AnyDesk.exe installs, node.exe spawned by msiexec, and outbound Ethereum RPC / secondary C2 from the same hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "camorreado.click" or ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "camorreado.click" or ProcessCommandLine has "v7.msi"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has "camorreado.click" or CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has "camorreado.click" or CommandLine has "v7.msi"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: EtherRAT MSI download via curl from camorreado.click
id: 7f3c2a1e-9b4d-4c8a-b2e1-3f5a6d7c8e90
description: Detects cmd/powershell spawning curl to download an MSI from the EtherRAT staging domain camorreado.click
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-cloud-bucket-hijacking.html
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-it-support-calls-on-microsoft-teams-push-etherrat-malware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\curl.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'camorreado.click'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\curl.exe OR *\\Curl.exe OR *\\CURL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*camorreado.click* OR *v7.msi*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\curl\.exe$/i
| regex("camorreado\.click", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=curl.exe (Processes.process=*camorreado.click* OR Processes.process=*v7.msi* OR Processes.process=*.msi*) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search process=*camorreado.click* OR process=*.msi* | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=curl.exe (Processes.process=*camorreado.click* OR Processes.process=*v7.msi* OR Processes.process=*.msi*) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search process=*camorreado.click* OR process=*.msi* | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
EtherRAT loader: msiexec runs v7.msi then node.exe executes staged JS runtime AIInstallation High
Hunts the second EtherRAT stage where msiexec executes the malicious MSI (v7.msi), which drops a legitimate Node.js runtime (v18.20.5) into a renamed directory and launches node.exe against an obfuscated JavaScript loader. Anchored on msiexec referencing the staging artefact and node.exe being spawned by msiexec/cmd from a user-writable path. Rationale: Unit 42 (corroborated by BleepingComputer) documents v7.msi staging Node.js v18.20.5 and running an obfuscated JS loader; node.exe parented by msiexec.exe from a temp/appdata path is a rare, campaign-specific chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-it-support-calls-on-microsoft-teams-push-etherrat-malware/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-leverage-microsoft-teams-call/
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1059.007 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit Node-based desktop apps (some Electron installers) launching node.exe from an MSI
  • Enterprise app packaging that bundles a private Node runtime via MSI
  • Developer toolchains invoking node from a temp build directory
  • VS Code / npm-installed global tools running node from AppData
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Code.exe","electron","nvm"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the MSI product/source is v#.msi from camorreado[.]click and inspect the node.exe command line and the JS file it points at (renamed runtime dir is a tell). 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate node.exe and msiexec children, quarantine the MSI and dropped runtime folder. 3) Hunt: look for Ethereum JSON-RPC / smart-contract lookups and secondary C2 egress from node.exe, plus HopToDesk/AnyDesk persistence on the same and peer hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "msiexec.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("camorreado.click","v7.msi"))

Teams-lure RMM install: HopToDesk + AnyDesk launched from Teams/browser AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the EtherRAT initial-access step where an actor impersonating a 'System Administrator' over a Microsoft Teams call abuses give/request control and directs the victim to install HopToDesk and AnyDesk for persistence. Anchored on these two specific RMM binaries executing with a Teams or browser parent. Rationale: Article and Register/CyberSecurityNews coverage name HopToDesk and AnyDesk as the RMM tools pushed via the Teams give/request-control lure; requiring a Teams/browser parent filters routine sanctioned RMM usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/07/07/fake-it-bods-on-microsoft-teams-coax-workers-into-installing-malware/5267610 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-leverage-microsoft-teams-call/
ATT&CKT1219 T1656 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit helpdesk that genuinely uses AnyDesk and instructs users to download it during a Teams call
  • End user installing HopToDesk/AnyDesk for personal remote access
  • MSP onboarding pushing AnyDesk via a browser download
  • AnyDesk auto-update relaunching itself (parent would be AnyDesk, filtered out)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","HopToDesk.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify whether the RMM install correlates with an inbound external/cross-tenant Teams call and an 'Employee Survey' phishing email to the same user; check if HopToDesk (uncommon in enterprise) is present. 2) Contain: uninstall the RMM tools, block their update/relay domains, isolate the host, and reset the user's credentials/sessions. 3) Hunt: pivot to curl→v7.msi and node.exe-from-msiexec activity on the host and check Teams admin logs for external control grants across other users.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("HopToDesk.exe","AnyDesk.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ms-teams.exe","Teams.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\HopToDesk.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\AnyDesk.exe"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ms-teams.exe","Teams.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Payment-SDK typosquat exfil: node/python egress to *.ngrok-free.dev from build host AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Socket-reported npm/PyPI typosquat campaign against Paysafe/Skrill/Neteller SDKs, which harvests developer secrets and tunnels them to an Ngrok endpoint (caliber-spinner-finishing[.]ngrok-free.dev). Anchored on package-manager/runtime processes (node/npm/python/pip) resolving or connecting to an ngrok-free.dev host. Rationale: Socket's write-up (corroborating THN) names caliber-spinner-finishing[.]ngrok-free.dev as the exfil endpoint; ngrok-free.dev egress initiated by a package manager/runtime on a build host is high-signal for supply-chain secret theft. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-pypi-campaign-typosquats-popular-secure-payment-apps • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-paysafe-skrill-sdks-on-npm-and-pypi-steal-credentials/
ATT&CKT1567 T1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using an ngrok tunnel to expose a local dev server
  • QA/webhook testing tools that resolve ngrok-free.dev
  • Node app with an ngrok SDK dependency used intentionally
  • Security researcher analysing the sample in a monitored VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ngrok" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--tunnel"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating node/npm/python process, capture its command line and the package installed just before the connection, and confirm the destination host (caliber-spinner-finishing[.]ngrok-free.dev). 2) Contain: block *.ngrok-free.dev at egress for build/CI segments, rotate any KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASS/AUTH/API env-var secrets present on the host, and remove the offending npm/PyPI package. 3) Hunt: search package-lock/requirements history for the 17 typosquatted Paysafe/Skrill/Neteller packages across all developer and CI hosts and review outbound to newly-seen ngrok subdomains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "ngrok-free.dev" or RemoteUrl has "caliber-spinner-finishing"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "ngrok-free.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Esri ArcGIS Server CVE-2026-9181 path traversal in REST Uploads resource AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated exploitation of CVE-2026-9181 (CVSS 9.8) in Esri ArcGIS Server ≤12.0, where crafted path parameters to the ArcGIS Server REST Uploads resource traverse outside the intended directory to read sensitive files. Anchored on web requests to the arcgis REST path containing directory-traversal sequences. Rationale: Article cites CVE-2026-9181 in the ArcGIS Server REST Uploads resource exploited via crafted path parameters (Horizon3.ai); traversal tokens (../, %2e%2e) against an arcgis REST/uploads URI is the concrete exploit signature. No Defender/Falcon/Datadog telemetry surfaces raw web-request URIs in this tenant, so those fields are left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-cloud-bucket-hijacking.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ArcGIS map service URLs that legitimately contain '..' in a layer/query string
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualus) probing ArcGIS endpoints
  • Encoded but benign relative paths in ArcGIS REST query parameters
  • Internal pentest/red-team validating the patch
Suppression filter
| where cIP !startswith "10." and cIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and the request returned 200/206 with an anomalous file path; check ArcGIS Server version against the ≤12.0 vulnerable range. 2) Contain: virtual-patch/WAF the REST Uploads endpoint, restrict it to authenticated access, and apply Esri's fixed build; block the offending source IP. 3) Hunt: review all successful traversal responses for which files were read (config, keystores, tokens), rotate exposed secrets, and correlate the source IP with follow-on auth or webshell-drop attempts.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has "arcgis"
| where csUriStem has "upload" or csUriStem has "rest"
| where csUriStem has_any ("..","%2e%2e","..%2f","%2e%2e%2f") or csUriQuery has_any ("..","%2e%2e","..%2f","%2e%2e%2f")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-9181", "CVE-2025-49760", "CVE-2025-59200", "CVE-2022-25477", "CVE-2022-25478", "CVE-2022-25479", "CVE-2022-25480", "CVE-2024-40431", "CVE-2024-40432")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-9181", "CVE-2025-49760", "CVE-2025-59200", "CVE-2022-25477", "CVE-2022-25478", "CVE-2022-25479", "CVE-2022-25480", "CVE-2024-40431", "CVE-2024-40432")

DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
