Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;

          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fc2907fa866f86e0821f75060a331ce69ee10ff3aa374587993b17ba5406fa33", "c2eeb74892408496f5a307a5b1fdc92d94fd014ab4252868f04046bf84718ab6", "94cb54d53927e4ba469099760db531be563a84d716df69e864062d90f0f2448d", "0cb2f7651d50e1ed1a691e82f0297d49444bdded2461e136cffb156d4f234e52", "c16784e2c7b3e3b798addd718850da18f8eb532ab8f352c769a4470d7124805d", "d46b4e8d188fe1773c44d38d730dcb6287639568240c765d9ad4ad79cd239e82"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-09 16 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

GigaWiper is a destructive backdoor that combines multiple wiping and ransomware-like capabilities into a single operational platform. This blog analyzes how the malware incorporates code from several previously separate malware families and provides guidance to help defenders detect and defend against similar threats. The post GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1047 T1053.005 T1059.001 T1190 T1486 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GigaWiper persistence: 'OneDrive Update' scheduled task run-every-minute · [LLM] GigaWiper persistence marker: HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment counter · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GigaWiper C2: RabbitMQ/Redis connection to 185.182.193.21:5544/7542 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GigaWiper destructive Golang backdoor/wiper by known SHA-256 · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
GigaWiper destructive Golang backdoor/wiper by known SHA-256 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution, drop, or load of the five Microsoft-published GigaWiper backdoor and standalone-wiper binaries. High-fidelity because these hashes are the destructive tooling itself (raw-disk wipe, Crucio-derived fake ransomware, FlockWiper re-implementation) - a single hit is an active destruction event. Rationale: Uses the five exact SHA-256 IOCs Microsoft published (Table 2) for the GigaWiper backdoor and standalone wiper; a hash match is unambiguous destructive tooling. Architecture corroborated by Binary Defense's BLUERABBIT (same RabbitMQ+Redis+dual-wiper design). Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/the-anatomy-of-wiper-malware-part-1/
ATT&CKT1485 T1561.002 T1561.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or IR team detonating a sample in a lab that reports to the same tenant
  • Threat-intel/EDR test harness deliberately dropping the IOC hashes to validate detections
  • Security vendor scan uploading the sample to a scanning appliance on the network
  • Re-hash collision is not credible for SHA-256, so genuine benign hits are near-zero
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malwarelab","detonation") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cuckoo.exe","procdump.exe"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the hash match and check DeviceProcessEvents for the process tree and whether WipeMain / schtasks 'OneDrive Update' / connections to 185.182.193.21 already followed - if any did, treat as live destruction, not a scan. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately network-isolate the host via Defender, force-block the five hashes tenant-wide, and snapshot/preserve any still-intact disks before the wiper reboots them. 3) HUNT: Sweep the tenant for the other four hashes, the 'OneDrive Update' task, HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment, and outbound traffic to 185.182.193.21:5544/7542 to find other beachheads before the fanout 'All' exchange broadcasts a wipe command.

union DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceFileEvents, DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in (GigaWiperHashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in (GigaWiperHashes)

| order by Timestamp desc

GigaWiper persistence: 'OneDrive Update' scheduled task run-every-minute AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of GigaWiper's persistence task, a schtasks invocation that registers a task literally named 'OneDrive Update' scheduled to run every minute plus at startup. Article-specific: real OneDrive uses tasks named 'OneDrive Standalone Update Task' under OneDrive.exe, never a per-minute 'OneDrive Update'. Rationale: Pins on the exact task name 'OneDrive Update' plus the per-minute schedule from the article's Figure 3 persistence command, and excludes genuine OneDrive updater parents - the masquerade name is the high-fidelity anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal software-distribution or RMM tool that names a custom task 'OneDrive Update' (rare; usually branded to the vendor)
  • Admin manually recreating a broken OneDrive updater task with a non-standard name
  • GPO/Intune deployment scripting a OneDrive keep-alive task per minute (should originate from a known deployment parent - allowlist it)
  • Backup/monitoring agent creating a minute-cadence task with 'OneDrive' in the name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft OneDrive\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\OneDrive"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the task XML (schtasks /query /tn 'OneDrive Update' /xml) and the InitiatingProcess hash - if the action points to an unsigned Golang PE or a non-OneDrive path, escalate. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the task (schtasks /delete /tn 'OneDrive Update' /f), isolate the host, and block the initiating binary's hash. 3) HUNT: Check HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment execution-counter value on this and peer hosts, and query for the five GigaWiper hashes and 185.182.193.21 connections to scope the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("/create", "OneDrive Update")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/sc minute", "/sc onstart", "minute")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe", "OneDriveSetup.exe", "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe", "msiexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_all ("/create", "OneDrive Update")
| where CommandLine has_any ("/sc minute", "/sc onstart", "minute")
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "\\OneDrive.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GigaWiper C2: RabbitMQ/Redis connection to 185.182.193.21:5544/7542 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to GigaWiper's hard-coded C2 host 185.182.193.21 on the RabbitMQ (AMQP 5544) and Redis (7542) ports it uses for command receipt and result upload. Article-specific: workstation processes speaking AMQP/Redis to a public IP on these non-standard ports is the backdoor's C2 heartbeat. Rationale: Uses Microsoft's exact hard-coded C2 IP 185.182.193.21 (ports 5544 RabbitMQ / 7542 Redis). The RabbitMQ-tasking + Redis-state design is independently corroborated by Binary Defense's BLUERABBIT, raising confidence in the pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities
ATT&CKT1071 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst or sinkhole researcher intentionally probing 185.182.193.21 from a monitored host
  • Firewall/IDS appliance sourcing a block-verification connection to the IOC IP
  • Shared-hosting reuse: the IP is later reassigned to a benign service (validate WHOIS/passive-DNS before trusting a stale IOC)
  • Legitimate internal RabbitMQ/Redis on a different IP is unaffected - this pins the specific malicious IP, not the ports alone
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify InitiatingProcess/ContextImageFileName making the connection - an unsigned Golang PE or a process also matching the GigaWiper hashes confirms C2. 2) CONTAIN: Block 185.182.193.21 at the firewall/EDR, isolate the beaconing host, and preserve memory before reboot (the wiper forces an immediate restart). 3) HUNT: Because commands publish to the fanout 'All' exchange (broadcast to every infected client), assume multiple hosts - sweep the tenant for any traffic to 185.182.193.21, the 'OneDrive Update' task, and the five GigaWiper hashes to enumerate all bots before a wipe is issued.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "185.182.193.21"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "185.182.193.21"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetworkProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GigaWiper C2 Connection to 185.182.193.21

GigaWiper persistence marker: HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment counter AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes to GigaWiper's execution-count registry value under HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment by a process that is not the genuine OneDrive client. Article-specific: real OneDrive stores state under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive, so a bare SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment key is a masqueraded first-run/run-count marker. Rationale: Anchors on the exact masqueraded persistence key HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment from the article, excluding genuine OneDrive writers - distinct from the real HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive path, so hits are high-fidelity. Falcon left empty: this non-ASEP HKCU value is not carried by FDR's AsepValueUpdate autostart telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities
ATT&CKT1112 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party OneDrive management/backup utility that writes state under a non-Microsoft OneDrive key
  • Legacy or renamed OneDrive build writing to SOFTWARE\OneDrive rather than SOFTWARE\Microsoft\OneDrive
  • Admin/registry-cleanup tooling touching an orphaned OneDrive key during troubleshooting
  • Endpoint-management agent snapshotting HKCU hives and re-writing values (writer would be the agent, not a Golang PE)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft OneDrive\\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the value data (it should be a small integer run-counter) and the writing process hash - correlate against the GigaWiper hash list and the 'OneDrive Update' task on the same host. 2) CONTAIN: If the writer is unsigned/Golang or hash-matched, isolate the host, delete the key, remove the task, and block the binary. 3) HUNT: The key is set to '0' on first run and incremented each scheduled execution - hosts with value > 0 have run repeatedly; pivot on those plus 185.182.193.21 traffic to find long-dwell infections.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe", "OneDriveSetup.exe", "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment"
| where ActingProcessName !has "OneDrive.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    object payload signature.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or SHA1 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or MD5 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or SHA1 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or MD5 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Forg365 phishing email to Cloudflare workers.dev lure via Amazon SES / SendGrid · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Forg365 device-code phishing: successful auth via Microsoft Authentication Broker · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Illicit OAuth app consent / permission grant during Forg365 takeover · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ForgCookie SSO token replay: non-interactive sign-in from a never-before-seen IP · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Malicious inbox rule created by a device-code-compromised Forg365 victim · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Forg365 device-code phishing: successful auth via Microsoft Authentication Broker AIExploitation High
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins that use the OAuth device-code flow against the Microsoft Authentication Broker (appId 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e), the core Forg365 initial-access path where a victim is tricked into authorizing an attacker-controlled device. Standard office users almost never complete device-code auth, so a success here is high-fidelity account takeover. Rationale: Anchors on the exact first-party app (Microsoft Authentication Broker / 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) plus the device-code protocol marker the article says to monitor in Entra logs. Success + this app is the single cleanest device-code-phishing signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/06/ai-enabled-device-code-phishing-campaign-april-2026/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/integrations/azure/initial_access_entra_id_oauth_device_code_phishing_tycoon_aitm • https://www.wiz.io/blog/recent-oauth-attacks-detection-strategies
ATT&CKT1566 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Conference-room / Teams-room service accounts enrolling via device code
  • Developers authenticating Azure CLI / az login --use-device-code on headless build agents
  • PowerShell/Graph automation using device-code grant in CI pipelines
  • IoT or digital-signage appliances legitimately completing device-code flow
  • Field staff enrolling a new mobile device via Authenticator broker
Suppression filter
| join kind=leftanti (AADSignInEventsBeta | where Timestamp between (ago(60d) .. ago(7d)) | where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" and AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" and ErrorCode == 0 | summarize Dc=count() by AccountUpn | where Dc > 5 | distinct AccountUpn) on AccountUpn
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the sign-in's IPAddress/Country and compare to the user's historical interactive locations; check whether the user role ever legitimately uses device-code flow. 2) Contain: if unexpected, revoke all refresh tokens/sessions (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession) and force MFA re-registration; block the source IP/ASN via Conditional Access. 3) Hunt: search the same AccountUpn for subsequent New-InboxRule, OAuth consent grants, and non-interactive sign-ins from the same IP (see companion UCs).

| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker

| where ErrorCode == 0                                            // successful auth only

          Application, ResourceDisplayName, DeviceTrustType, IsInteractive, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs

| where ResultType == 0

          AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, AutonomousSystemNumber
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Forg365 phishing email to Cloudflare workers.dev lure via Amazon SES / SendGrid AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound business-document lure emails delivered through Amazon SES (with SendGrid-hosted tracking images) that link to the Forg365 Cloudflare Pages landing page electrical-fuchsia-cod.workers.dev, or that originate from the sender domain logfriend.com. Targets the specific delivery infrastructure ZeroBEC attributes to this campaign. Rationale: Uses the pre-extracted campaign IOCs (electrical-fuchsia-cod.workers.dev landing page, logfriend.com sender) plus the article's stated delivery stack (Amazon SES + SendGrid). The specific workers.dev host makes the email join and the endpoint DNS pivot high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-forg365-phishing-platform-uses-ai-to-target-microsoft-365-accounts/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/debull-tooling-abuses-microsoft-device.html
ATT&CKT1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SaaS apps hosted on *.workers.dev that staff receive links to
  • Marketing/newsletter senders legitimately using Amazon SES + SendGrid tracking pixels
  • A partner whose brand really is on logfriend.com (verify SPF/DKIM/DMARC in AuthenticationDetails)
  • Internal red-team phishing simulations using Cloudflare Pages
  • Bug-bounty/security researcher relaying a sample of the lure internally
Suppression filter
| where not(SenderFromDomain in~ ("your-known-saas-vendor.com")) and AuthenticationDetails !has "pass"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm DeliveryAction (Delivered vs Junked) and pull recipient list; check AuthenticationDetails for SPF/DKIM/DMARC fails on logfriend.com/SES. 2) Contain: soft-delete the message org-wide (Search-Mailbox / purge), block electrical-fuchsia-cod.workers.dev and logfriend.com at the proxy/mail gateway, add both to tenant block list. 3) Hunt: correlate any recipient who resolved the workers.dev host (Falcon DNS) with a subsequent Microsoft Authentication Broker device-code sign-in (UC1).
let LookbackDays = 14d;

| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, SenderFromDomain,

| order by Timestamp desc

Malicious inbox rule created by a device-code-compromised Forg365 victim AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates Entra device-code sign-ins against the Microsoft Authentication Broker with subsequent mailbox-rule creation/modification by the same account, catching the Forg365 post-compromise step where operators plant hiding/forwarding rules and keyword-monitoring in captured mailboxes. The device-code linkage removes the noise of routine inbox-rule activity. Rationale: Chains the article's named initial-access mechanism (device code via Authentication Broker) to its named post-compromise action (mailbox rules), so it only fires on accounts that actually took the Forg365 path — far cleaner than a standalone inbox-rule rule. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-forg365-phishing-platform-uses-ai-to-target-microsoft-365-accounts/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/recent-oauth-attacks-detection-strategies
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user who legitimately uses device-code flow (kiosk/dev) then sets up a normal vacation/forwarding rule
  • Admin-created transport/inbox rules during mailbox migration coinciding with a device-code enrollment
  • Outlook mobile creating a client-side rule after a broker token refresh
  • Help-desk remediating a mailbox and adding a sweep rule
Suppression filter
| where not(ActionType == "Set-InboxRule" and RawEventData has "AutoReply")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the rule Parameters/RawEventData - look for forward-to-external, delete-on-arrival, or keyword move-to-folder actions typical of Forg365 keyword monitoring. 2) Contain: delete the malicious rule, revoke the user's sessions/refresh tokens, reset credentials, disable device-code flow for the user. 3) Hunt: enumerate all rules across recently device-code-authenticated accounts; check OAuth consent grants and non-interactive token replay (UC4, UC5) for the same identities.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let DeviceCodeVictims = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | distinct AccountObjectId;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType in~ ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| where AccountObjectId in (DeviceCodeVictims)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let DeviceCodeVictims = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
    | where ResultType == 0
    | distinct UserPrincipalName;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where Operation in~ ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| where UserId in~ (DeviceCodeVictims)
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, ClientIP, OriginatingServer, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where Change.action=modified (Change.command="New-InboxRule" OR Change.command="Set-InboxRule" OR Change.command="UpdateInboxRules") by Change.user Change.object Change.src Change.command
| `drop_dm_object_name(Change)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where Change.action=modified (Change.command="New-InboxRule" OR Change.command="Set-InboxRule" OR Change.command="UpdateInboxRules") by Change.user Change.object Change.src Change.command
| `drop_dm_object_name(Change)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Illicit OAuth app consent / permission grant during Forg365 takeover AIInstallation Medium
Hunts application consent grants and delegated-permission additions in Entra ID, the mechanism Forg365 uses to register attacker OAuth apps (and the ForgCookie backend flow) for persistent, re-auth-free access to Microsoft services. The article explicitly instructs defenders to investigate unexpected OAuth grants. Rationale: Directly implements the article's remediation guidance to investigate OAuth grants; Forg365 configures attacker OAuth apps and the ForgCookie backend triggers silent OAuth flows, so consent/permission-grant events are the persistence choke point. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-forg365-phishing-platform-uses-ai-to-target-microsoft-365-accounts/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/recent-oauth-attacks-detection-strategies
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admins onboarding a legitimate enterprise app (bulk consent)
  • Users granting consent to sanctioned productivity add-ins
  • Automated provisioning of first-party Microsoft apps
  • MSP/CSP delegated-admin app assignments
  • Developers registering test apps in a dev tenant
Suppression filter
| where TargetApp !in~ ("Microsoft Graph","Office 365 Exchange Online") and Result == "success"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect TargetApp - is the app newly registered, an unverified publisher, or requesting high-value scopes (Mail.ReadWrite, offline_access)? Cross-check the Actor against device-code victims (UC1). 2) Contain: revoke the service principal's grants (Remove-MgOauth2PermissionGrant), disable/delete the app registration, revoke user sessions. 3) Hunt: review all consents in the window from the same ActorIp/ASN, and look for Graph API mailbox access from the granted app.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in~ ("Consent to application","Add delegated permission grant","Add app role assignment to service principal")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, IPAddress, CountryCode, ObjectName, ActivityObjects, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in~ ("Consent to application","Add delegated permission grant","Add app role assignment to service principal","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ActorIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| extend TargetApp = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorIp, TargetApp, Result, CorrelationId, TargetResources
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ForgCookie SSO token replay: non-interactive sign-in from a never-before-seen IP AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts successful NON-interactive Entra sign-ins for a user from an IP that never appears in that user's interactive sign-in history over 30 days - the signature of the Forg365 ForgCookie extension / AiTM proxy silently refreshing stolen SSO cookies from attacker infrastructure. Provides persistent access without re-authentication. Rationale: Models the ForgCookie extension behaviour described in the article (clears cookies, triggers silent OAuth to capture fresh SSO cookies) as bursts of non-interactive token usage from an IP absent from the user's interactive baseline - a clean AiTM cookie-replay pivot distinct from the interactive device-code signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-forg365-phishing-platform-uses-ai-to-target-microsoft-365-accounts/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/06/ai-enabled-device-code-phishing-campaign-april-2026/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate VPN / SASE egress that differs from the user's home interactive IP
  • Mobile carrier NAT rotating IPs during background mail sync
  • Legitimate travel where interactive login happened on a device not seen in baseline
  • New office/branch egress IP not yet in the 30-day baseline
  • Cloud-hosted mailbox integrations (backup, archiving) refreshing tokens
Suppression filter
| where Country != "" and not(IPAddress startswith "10." or IPAddress startswith "192.168." or IPAddress startswith "172.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: geolocate the new IP/ASN and compare to the user's Country/interactive history; check whether the AppDisplayName set includes Exchange/Graph/SharePoint (broad token brokering). 2) Contain: if unexplained, revoke all refresh tokens/sessions immediately, force re-auth, and add the IP/ASN to a Conditional Access block. 3) Hunt: pivot the same IP across all users for shared attacker infrastructure, and correlate with device-code sign-ins (UC1) and inbox-rule/OAuth activity (UC3/UC4).
let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where ErrorCode == 0 and IsInteractive == true
    | summarize by AccountUpn, IPAddress;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0 and IsInteractive == false
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountUpn, IPAddress
| summarize SignIns = count(), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 8), Apps = make_set(Application, 8),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Country = any(Country)
        by AccountUpn, IPAddress
| where SignIns > 3   // 3 = tolerate transient CDN/proxy token refreshes on legit travel (P95 baseline)
| order by SignIns desc
let Baseline = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where ResultType == 0 and IsInteractive == true
    | summarize by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == 0
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| summarize SignIns = count(), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 8), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 8),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Loc = any(Location)
        by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| where SignIns > 3   // 3 = strip one-off travel token refreshes; tune per tenant
| order by SignIns desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user Authentication.src _time
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| eventstats values(src) as interactive_src by user
| where NOT src IN (interactive_src)
| stats count as signins values(src) as new_src min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by user
| where signins > 3
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user Authentication.src _time
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| eventstats values(src) as interactive_src by user
| where NOT src IN (interactive_src)
| stats count as signins values(src) as new_src min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by user
| where signins > 3

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

SecurityEvent

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
