Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:

    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — One Target, Two Flags | Rival Espionage Actors Converge On Pakistani Law Enforce
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement · [LLM] Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement AICommand & Control High
Hunts any internal host establishing outbound connections to the 13 C2 IPs SentinelLABS attributed to the four tooling clusters (PlugX, ShadowPad, Cobalt Strike, Remcos) converging on Balochistan Police and other Pakistani law-enforcement orgs between Feb 2024 and Apr 2026. Pure network-IOC match on disclosed espionage C2 servers. Rationale: Anchored on the exact 13 C2 IPs from Table 1 / code blocks (PlugX 172.111.233.x + 172.94.9.x + 45.74.6.17, ShadowPad 45.125.32.218, Cobalt Strike 142.171.183.8 + 193.42.25.65, Remcos 89.31.121.220). Any egress to these known-bad hosts is high-fidelity; the tooling families and Pakistani-entity victimology are corroborated externally, though the specific IPs are from the SentinelLABS primary report only. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad • https://thehackernews.com/2023/07/pakistani-entities-targeted-in.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-intel analyst deliberately sandboxing or sinkholing one of these IPs from a corporate host
  • IP reassignment after takedown — a benign service later hosted on a recycled VPS IP (172.94.9.x / 45.x hosting ranges are commodity VPS)
  • Internal threat-intel validation tooling or EDR connectivity checks pinging the IOC list
  • Proxy/NAT concentration causing many internal hosts to appear as one src toward the IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") // exclude EDR/AV connectivity-check processes
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connection is genuinely outbound and established (not a blocked/attempt), identify the initiating process and host role — servers hosting the CMS/FIR/HRMIS/HotelEye/CRMS apps are highest priority. 2) Contain: block all 13 IPs at perimeter, isolate the host, snapshot memory before reboot to preserve PlugX/ShadowPad in-memory implants. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for DLL side-loading (unsigned DLL next to a signed EXE), scheduled tasks/Run keys created near first-seen, and lateral SMB/RDP from the host; sweep the org for any other host touching the same /24s (172.111.233.0/24, 172.94.9.0/24).

Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) AICommand & Control Medium
Tighter server-side pivot: a web/application-server process (IIS w3wp, Apache/Tomcat java, nginx, php-cgi) on a Pakistani law-enforcement web server initiating outbound to the disclosed C2 IPs. Grounds on the article's China-nexus 'custom implants masquerading as a portal update' planted in one of the citizen/police web applications (e.g. the Complaint Management System). Rationale: Combines the exact C2 IP set with a server-process filter to isolate the article's specific scenario — a China-nexus implant planted in a citizen/police web application (CMS) beaconing out. Web-server processes reaching commodity-VPS C2 IPs is extremely rare and high-fidelity, and directly targets the compromised-webapp vector the article calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1505.003 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web app legitimately calling an outbound API that happens to be on a recycled VPS IP after IOC takedown
  • Java-based agent/monitoring on the web server making outbound telemetry calls
  • Server-side update/package fetch (Tomcat/Maven, php composer) to a mirror on the same hosting range
  • App-server health-check or CDN origin-pull to a reassigned address
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "maven" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "composer" // exclude server package-manager fetches
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which web application the process serves (CMS/FIR/HRMIS/AVLS/HotelEye/CRMS) and whether the beacon started after a recent 'portal update'/deployment window; review web-root for recently modified/added handler, JSP, ASPX or PHP files. 2) Contain: take the web app offline or block egress, preserve IIS/Tomcat logs and web-root for forensics, rotate app/service and DB credentials the server can reach. 3) Hunt: search web access logs (W3CIISLog/AppServiceHTTPLogs) for the implant's request pattern, look for webshell-style POSTs, and pivot to any DB export or biometric/criminal-record access from the compromised app identity.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Microsoft Defender engine (MsMpEng.exe) spawns shell/LOLBin — RoguePlanet CVE-2026-50656 exploitation AIExploitation High
Hunts the RoguePlanet privilege-escalation signature: the Antimalware Service Executable (MsMpEng.exe), which hosts the vulnerable mpengine.dll, spawning an interactive shell, scripting host, or LOLBin. MsMpEng.exe legitimately spawns only conhost.exe/MpCmdRun.exe, so a cmd/powershell child is the near-unique fingerprint of the TOCTOU race being won to land a SYSTEM shell. Rationale: MsMpEng.exe is the process that loads the vulnerable mpengine.dll; it never legitimately spawns cmd/powershell/scripting hosts, so this parent->child pair is a near-zero-FP fingerprint of the RoguePlanet SYSTEM-shell primitive. Cross-checked MSRC advisory, Morphisec and CloudSEK write-ups plus the Elastic 'Suspicious Microsoft Antimalware Service Execution' rule shape. Cross-checked against: • https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2026-50656 • https://www.morphisec.com/blog/microsoft-defender-zero-day-rogueplanet-when-your-detector-becomes-the-attack-surface/ • https://www.cloudsek.com/blog/redsun-windows-0day-when-defender-becomes-the-attacker • https://detection.fyi/elastic/detection-rules/windows/defense_evasion_execution_windefend_unusual_path/
ATT&CKT1068 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Purple-team / Atomic Red Team simulation of Defender-parented process execution
  • Security researcher detonating the public RoguePlanet PoC in a lab image
  • Telemetry mis-attribution where a re-parented process is incorrectly linked to MsMpEng.exe during heavy scan load
  • Third-party AV/EDR management wrappers that shim into the Defender service host (rare)
  • Defender troubleshooting via MpCmdRun.exe legitimately launching conhost (excluded by the child allowlist)
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("MpCmdRun.exe","conhost.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "AtomicRedTeam"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull ProcessIntegrityLevel, AccountName and full ProcessCommandLine of the child — a System/High integrity cmd or powershell child of MsMpEng.exe on a standard user's box is a confirmed SYSTEM-shell escalation. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and force the Defender engine to update to >=1.1.26060.3008 (MpCmdRun.exe -SignatureUpdate). 3) Hunt: on the same host, timeline all subsequent SYSTEM-context actions (new local admins, service installs, LSASS access); sweep the org for other MsMpEng.exe->shell events and for hosts still below engine 1.1.26060.3008.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MsMpEng.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessIntegrityLevel, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\MsMpEng.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\net.exe","\\whoami.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Microsoft Defender MsMpEng.exe Spawns Shell or LOLBin (RoguePlanet CVE-2026-50656)
id: 6a1f0d3e-8c22-4a7b-9b1e-2f5c0a9d7e41
description: Detects the Antimalware Service Executable (MsMpEng.exe) spawning an interactive shell, scripting host, or LOLBin, the exploitation fingerprint of the RoguePlanet TOCTOU privilege-escalation flaw in mpengine.dll.
references:
  - https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2026-50656
  - https://www.morphisec.com/blog/microsoft-defender-zero-day-rogueplanet-when-your-detector-becomes-the-attack-surface/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.t1211
  - attack.privilege_escalation
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\MsMpEng.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\net.exe'
      - '\whoami.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\MsMpEng.exe OR *\msmpeng.exe OR *\MSMPENG.EXE) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\rundll32.exe OR *\regsvr32.exe OR *\net.exe OR *\whoami.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/MsMpEng\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|net|whoami)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, IntegrityLevel], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="MsMpEng.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_integrity_level | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="MsMpEng.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_integrity_level | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Hosts running vulnerable Microsoft Malware Protection Engine below 1.1.26060.3008 (RoguePlanet exposure) AIExploitation High
Surfaces endpoints still exposed to RoguePlanet (CVE-2026-50656) by enumerating devices where TVM maps the CVE or the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine build is older than the fixed 1.1.26060.3008. The exploit works with real-time protection on or off, so patch-state exposure is the only reliable mitigation signal. Rationale: Uses the concrete fixed engine version (1.1.26060.3008) and CVE id from the article/MSRC to convert 'are we exposed' into a deployable posture query via the TVM vulnerability table / CIM Vulnerabilities datamodel. Because RoguePlanet ignores real-time-protection state, engine build is the authoritative exposure signal. Cross-checked against: • https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2026-50656 • https://threatprotect.qualys.com/2026/06/18/microsoft-defender-zero-day-vulnerability-exploited-in-attacks-cve-2026-50656-rogueplanet/
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Devices already auto-updated but TVM inventory not yet refreshed (stale snapshot, ~24h lag)
  • Air-gapped/offline hosts that report an old engine build but cannot be reached by attackers
  • Golden images captured pre-patch that are never actually deployed
  • Duplicate DeviceId entries from re-imaged machines inflating the exposed count
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank exposed devices by internet-facing / privileged-user status using DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing and logged-on admins. 2) Contain: trigger an on-demand engine update (MpCmdRun.exe -SignatureUpdate or ADR/Intune) to move builds to >=1.1.26060.3008; verify with a follow-up TVM query. 3) Hunt: on any host that stayed unpatched >72h, run UC-1 (MsMpEng.exe->shell) retroactively over that window to confirm no exploitation already occurred.

| where CveId == "CVE-2026-50656"
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-50656"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc

RoguePlanet PoC (github.com/MSNightmare/RoguePlanet) download or execution AIDelivery Medium
Hunts ingress and execution of the public RoguePlanet proof-of-concept by matching command lines referencing the MSNightmare/RoguePlanet repository or its build/binary artifacts. Catches an operator cloning, downloading, or running the exploit before the MsMpEng.exe->shell behaviour fires. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC repository path (MSNightmare/RoguePlanet) named as an IOC in the article plus derived build/binary artifact names, giving a delivery-stage pivot distinct from the runtime behaviour in UC-1. Repo path is specific enough to keep FPs to research/patch-testing activity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-patches-rogueplanet-defender.html • https://undercodetesting.com/nightmare-eclipse-strikes-again-rogueplanet-0-day-exploit-grants-system-access-on-fully-patched-windows-are-you-protected-video/
ATT&CKT1105 T1588.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised red team / patch-validation teams cloning the PoC to verify remediation
  • Threat-intel analysts saving the repo name into notes or ticket automation that echoes into a command line
  • Security tooling that ingests IOC lists containing the string RoguePlanet
  • EDR content-testing pipelines referencing the artifact name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "patch-validation" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host/user is sanctioned for exploit research; inspect the parent process (git.exe, powershell.exe, browser download helper) and destination path of the artifact. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, quarantine the RoguePlanet artifact, and preserve the binary hash. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC-1 on the same host to see whether the PoC was actually run (MsMpEng.exe->shell), and check the engine build for pre-patch exposure.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("MSNightmare/RoguePlanet","RoguePlanet.exe","RoguePlanet-main","RoguePlanet.sln")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("MSNightmare/RoguePlanet","RoguePlanet.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("MSNightmare/RoguePlanet","RoguePlanet.exe","RoguePlanet-main","RoguePlanet.sln")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50656")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50656")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GodDamn Ransomware Uses PoisonX Driver to Disable Endpoint Defenses

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 16 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a new ransomware family called GodDamn that employs the PoisonX kernel driver to neutralize security software as part of its defense evasion strategy. According to a new report published by the Threat Hunter Team from Symantec, the ransomware was first publicly spotted in the wild on May 21, 2026. It's assessed to be a rebrand of the Beast ransomware,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GodDamn Ransomware Uses PoisonX Driver to Disable Endpoint Defenses
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PoisonX BYOVD kernel driver (g11.sys) load / drop by GodDamn ransomware · [LLM] Masquerading 'symantec.exe' user-mode EDR-killer (fake Symantec company info) · [LLM] AnyDesk deployed as silent auto-start service (GodDamn reusable installer) · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NirSoft-based credential harvesting toolkit execution (browsers, VNC, Wi-Fi, mail, sniffer) · [LLM] GodDamn ransomware mass file rename to .God8Damn extension · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
PoisonX BYOVD kernel driver (g11.sys) load / drop by GodDamn ransomware AIInstallation High
Hunts the load or drop of the Microsoft-signed malicious PoisonX kernel driver 'g11.sys' that GodDamn (Hyadina/Beast rebrand) uses in a bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver attack to blind EDR from kernel space. Pivots on the exact driver filename plus the article's file hash rather than a generic BYOVD template. Rationale: g11.sys is the exact PoisonX driver filename named in the article and confirmed across Symantec/GentleKiller reporting; combined with the pre-extracted SHA256 this is a named-binary indicator with near-zero legitimate occurrence. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html • https://securityaffairs.com/193941/malware/inside-gentlekiller-the-edr-killer-powering-the-gentlemen.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1211 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party driver coincidentally named g11.sys (rare — verify Microsoft signature + WHQL status and cross-check the SHA256)
  • Security-vendor sandbox/detonation host loading the sample for analysis
  • Purple-team BYOVD exercise dropping the same driver
  • Threat-intel/malware-research workstation with the sample on disk
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loaded module is g11.sys and pull SHA256; if it matches a90c3433... treat as confirmed BYOVD. Identify InitiatingProcess and account. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the driver hash via ASR/WDAC, and add g11.sys to the Microsoft Vulnerable Driver Blocklist; kernel-level EDR blinding means the host is likely already partially uninstrumented. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for g11.sys and symantec.exe, for AnyDesk service installs, and for NirSoft credential-harvester execution on the same and adjacent hosts (this actor stages ransomware after EDR is neutralized).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "g11.sys"
    or SHA256 == "a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4697, 7045)
| where ServiceFileName has "g11.sys"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PoisonX Malicious Kernel Driver g11.sys Load (GodDamn Ransomware BYOVD)
id: 5f2a9c14-6d3b-4e77-9a1c-2b8f0c7e4d10
description: Detects load or presence of the Microsoft-signed malicious PoisonX driver g11.sys used by GodDamn/Hyadina ransomware to disable EDR from kernel space.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.t1211
  - attack.t1543.003
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_name:
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\g11.sys'
  selection_hash:
    Hashes|contains: 'SHA256=A90C3433006CDEDFBB135718F309209C0699CB097D4A55E85357130D5EC689B3'
  condition: selection_name or selection_hash
level: high
source:windows.sysmon (@TargetFilename:(*\\g11.sys OR *\\G11.sys OR *\\G11.SYS) OR @Hashes:*A90C3433006CDEDFBB135718F309209C0699CB097D4A55E85357130D5EC689B3*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\g11\.sys$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

Masquerading 'symantec.exe' user-mode EDR-killer (fake Symantec company info) AIInstallation High
Hunts the GodDamn user-mode defense-evasion tool that impersonates a Symantec product by naming itself symantec.exe while carrying no genuine Symantec/Broadcom version metadata. Excludes real Symantec/Broadcom-signed binaries to isolate the impostor killer. Rationale: The article explicitly states the killer is 'dressed as a Symantec product (symantec.exe)'; a process named symantec.exe with non-Symantec/Broadcom company metadata (or run from a non-standard path) is a high-fidelity masquerade indicator with minimal legitimate footprint. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver.html • https://thomasharris6.wordpress.com/2026/07/09/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver-to-disable-endpoint-defenses/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Symantec/Broadcom Endpoint Protection helper running from a non-standard install path
  • SCCM/Intune packaging that renames a legit Symantec installer to symantec.exe (check signature)
  • Internal IT wrapper script named symantec.exe for AV troubleshooting
  • Security-tool inventory scanner labelled symantec.exe
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Symantec","Broadcom")) and FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the file's digital signature and CompanyName; a valid Broadcom/Symantec Authenticode signature clears it, an unsigned or mismatched binary confirms the killer. Check FolderPath (Temp/ProgramData/Public = suspicious). 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the SHA256, and verify EDR agent processes are still running and reporting. 3) Hunt: on confirmation, look on the same host for g11.sys (PoisonX), AnyDesk service install, and NirSoft harvester execution — symantec.exe typically runs immediately before the encryptor.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "symantec.exe"
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Symantec", "Broadcom"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\symantec.exe"
| where NewProcessName !contains "\\Program Files\\Symantec"
     and NewProcessName !contains "\\Program Files\\Broadcom"
     and NewProcessName !contains "\\Program Files (x86)\\Symantec"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Masquerading symantec.exe EDR-Killer (GodDamn Ransomware)

NirSoft-based credential harvesting toolkit execution (browsers, VNC, Wi-Fi, mail, sniffer) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the NirSoft-derived credential harvester GodDamn operators run before deploying ransomware, which pulls secrets from browsers, Windows Credential Manager, VNC, email clients, Wi-Fi profiles and live network traffic. Pivots on the specific NirSoft tool filenames and the 'NirSoft' version-info company string. Rationale: The article's description of the harvester (browsers + Credential Manager + cached domain creds + VNC + email + Wi-Fi + live traffic) maps precisely onto the NirSoft tool family; matching those specific binary names and the 'NirSoft' CompanyName isolates the toolkit while smartsniff.exe covers the 'live network traffic' capability. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver.html • https://thomasharris6.wordpress.com/2026/07/09/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver-to-disable-endpoint-defenses/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1555 T1040 T1003.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately recovering a forgotten Wi-Fi/VNC/browser password with a NirSoft utility
  • Help-desk credential-recovery workflow
  • Penetration test using NirSoft tooling
  • Forensics/DFIR analyst running these tools on an evidence host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","anydesk.exe") or IsInitiatingProcessRemoteSession == true
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user context — an interactive admin recovering one password differs from a burst of multiple NirSoft tools launched by a scripted/remote parent (powershell/cmd/psexec). Check parent process and whether output files (e.g. .txt/.csv dumps) were written. 2) Contain: isolate the host and force-reset every credential class the tools can reach (domain, browser-saved, VNC, Wi-Fi PSKs) for affected accounts. 3) Hunt: pivot to co-located symantec.exe / g11.sys / AnyDesk deployment on the host and to any PsExec-driven spread to adjacent hosts; harvested creds fuel this actor's lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName =~ "NirSoft"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "NirSoft"
    or FileName in~ ("webbrowserpassview.exe","mailpv.exe","vncpassview.exe","wirelesskeyview.exe","netpass.exe","iepv.exe","chromepass.exe","passwordfox.exe","netresview.exe","credentialsfileview.exe","smartsniff.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("webbrowserpassview.exe","mailpv.exe","vncpassview.exe","wirelesskeyview.exe","netpass.exe","iepv.exe","chromepass.exe","passwordfox.exe","netresview.exe","credentialsfileview.exe","smartsniff.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AnyDesk deployed as silent auto-start service (GodDamn reusable installer) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts GodDamn's persistence/remote-access step: AnyDesk installed unattended with auto-start-on-boot and a preset password, frequently launched by a pre-staged PowerShell installer and registered as a Windows service to survive reboots. Pivots on AnyDesk's specific unattended install flags rather than mere AnyDesk presence. Rationale: The article states AnyDesk was set up on each host and 'registered as an auto-start Windows service' via a pre-staged PowerShell installer; AnyDesk invoked with --install/--start-with-win/--silent/--set-password is the concrete unattended-deployment signature that separates attacker staging from an interactive user launch. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver.html • https://thomasharris6.wordpress.com/2026/07/09/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver-to-disable-endpoint-defenses/
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP/IT department deploying AnyDesk fleet-wide via its own silent installer and GPO
  • Sanctioned unattended AnyDesk rollout with --start-with-win for remote support
  • Software packaging system (SCCM/Intune) installing AnyDesk
  • AnyDesk auto-update re-registering the service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has "--set-password"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm AnyDesk is not a sanctioned remote-support tool in this environment; check the parent process (a powershell.exe/cmd.exe pre-staged installer parent is a strong attacker signal) and whether --set-password was used to plant an attacker-controlled unattended password. 2) Contain: stop and disable the AnyDesk service, block the AnyDesk client, and pull AnyDesk connection logs (ad.trace / connection_trace.txt) to identify the attacker relay ID/IP. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts with the same silent-install signature (article reports ~10 hosts in one org) and correlate with PsExec activity, symantec.exe, g11.sys and reboot sequences that follow each install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "anydesk.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--install", "--start-with-win", "--silent", "--set-password")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\anydesk.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--install", "--start-with-win", "--silent", "--set-password")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GodDamn ransomware mass file rename to .God8Damn extension AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the encryption/impact stage where GodDamn renames victim files with the .God8Damn extension at scale. Uses a per-host mass-rename threshold on the article-specific extension to turn the impact event into an alertable signal. Rationale: .God8Damn is the article's named encryption extension for Hyadina/GodDamn attacks; a single host renaming 20+ files to that extension is an unambiguous encryption-in-progress indicator with essentially no legitimate cause. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver.html • https://thomasharris6.wordpress.com/2026/07/09/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver-to-disable-endpoint-defenses/
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate application or user coincidentally saving files with a .God8Damn suffix (implausible at 20+ files)
  • Backup/restore of already-encrypted files from a prior incident replaying the extension
  • Malware-analysis host detonating the sample
  • IR team restaging encrypted samples for triage
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the InitiatingProcess doing the renames and its SHA256; encryption is already underway, so speed matters. Identify the scope (single share vs many hosts). 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host from the network, kill the encrypting process, disable the compromised account, and protect/segment backups and file shares before the encryptor reaches them. 3) Hunt: this actor also renames files with the victim's name as the extension on some segments, so also hunt for a sudden burst of files sharing one novel extension org-wide; back-trace to symantec.exe/g11.sys EDR-kill and AnyDesk footholds and check the qTox/email ransom note drop.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".God8Damn" or PreviousFileName endswith ".God8Damn"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FileName), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where FileCount >= 20   // 20 = mass-rename threshold to strip single-file noise
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".God8Damn" or TargetFileExtension =~ "God8Damn"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFileName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| where FileCount >= 20   // 20 = mass-rename threshold to strip single-file noise
| order by LastSeen desc
title: GodDamn Ransomware .God8Damn Encrypted File Extension

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

            - 'invoke-expression'

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or SHA1 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or MD5 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or SHA1 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or MD5 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Defender engine (MsMpEng.exe) overwriting System32\wermgr.exe — RoguePlanet CVE-2026-50656 AIInstallation High
Hunts the core RoguePlanet privilege-escalation primitive: the Defender scanning engine (MsMpEng.exe) winning a TOCTOU race and writing/replacing C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe with the attacker payload. The Defender engine legitimately quarantines to its own store and never writes an executable into System32, so this is a near-zero-baseline exploitation signal. Rationale: Uses the exact exploit primitive corroborated by external write-ups: the Defender engine binary MsMpEng.exe writing into C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe. Both the writing process and the target path are fixed, article-specific values with effectively no legitimate occurrence. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-patches-rogueplanet-defender.html • https://www.morphisec.com/blog/microsoft-defender-zero-day-rogueplanet-when-your-detector-becomes-the-attack-surface/ • https://threatprotect.qualys.com/2026/06/18/microsoft-defender-zero-day-vulnerability-exploited-in-attacks-cve-2026-50656-rogueplanet/
ATT&CKT1068 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Defender legitimately flagging a genuinely-infected wermgr.exe and quarantining it (write would target the quarantine store, not overwrite System32 — verify FolderPath)
  • Windows feature/servicing update replacing wermgr.exe via TiWorker.exe/TrustedInstaller (parent would NOT be MsMpEng.exe)
  • Security researcher / red-team validating the PoC in a lab
  • EDR file-event path normalization mislabeling the initiating process during a Defender platform update
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "Quarantine" and FolderPath !has "Windows Defender"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is MsMpEng.exe and the target is literally C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe (not the quarantine path); pull SHA256 of the new wermgr.exe and compare to the Microsoft-signed baseline. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any wermgr.exe-spawned SYSTEM shells, and restore the legitimate signed wermgr.exe; verify Malware Protection Engine is >= 1.1.26060.3008. 3) Hunt: search the host for wermgr.exe spawning cmd/powershell (UC2), manual triggers of the Windows Error Reporting scheduled task, and other System32 binaries recently written by MsMpEng.exe.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "wermgr.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\System32\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MsMpEng.exe"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "wermgr.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\System32\"
| where ActingProcessName has "MsMpEng.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Defender Engine Overwrites System32 wermgr.exe (RoguePlanet CVE-2026-50656)
id: 8f3c1a42-7b6e-4d29-9c0a-2e6b1f4a9d11
description: MsMpEng.exe (Microsoft Malware Protection Engine) writing to System32\wermgr.exe indicates abuse of the CVE-2026-50656 remediation race condition.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/microsoft/microsoft-patches-rogueplanet-defender-zero-day-vulnerability/
  - https://www.morphisec.com/blog/microsoft-defender-zero-day-rogueplanet-when-your-detector-becomes-the-attack-surface/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\MsMpEng.exe'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\System32\wermgr.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\MsMpEng.exe OR *\\msmpeng.exe OR *\\MSMPENG.EXE) @TargetFilename:(*\\System32\\wermgr.exe OR *\\System32\\WERMGR.EXE OR *\\system32\\wermgr.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/MsMpEng\.exe$/i TargetFileName=/wermgr\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="wermgr.exe" Filesystem.file_path="*\\System32\\wermgr.exe" Filesystem.process_name="MsMpEng.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="wermgr.exe" Filesystem.file_path="*\\System32\\wermgr.exe" Filesystem.process_name="MsMpEng.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Trojanized wermgr.exe spawning SYSTEM command shell — RoguePlanet privilege escalation AIExploitation High
Hunts the RoguePlanet payoff: the overwritten C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe (executed via the Windows Error Reporting scheduled task) spawning cmd.exe/powershell.exe as SYSTEM. Legitimate wermgr.exe handles Windows Error Reporting and launches WerFault, never an interactive shell. Rationale: Anchors on the concrete post-exploitation behavior confirmed across sources: System32 wermgr.exe (the WER handler) launching an interactive SYSTEM shell. The parent binary and its System32 path are fixed article-specific values; legitimate wermgr.exe never spawns cmd/powershell. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-patches-rogueplanet-defender.html • https://www.rescana.com/post/cve-2026-50656-microsoft-defender-rogueplanet-zero-day-enables-local-privilege-escalation-on-fully-patched-windows-10-11 • https://www.morphisec.com/blog/microsoft-defender-zero-day-rogueplanet-when-your-detector-becomes-the-attack-surface/
ATT&CKT1068 T1053.005 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/debug session where wermgr.exe is manually invoked to inspect Windows Error Reporting (extremely rare)
  • Third-party crash-reporting tooling renaming its own binary to wermgr.exe (verify signature/path)
  • Red-team or PoC validation of RoguePlanet in a lab
  • EDR mis-parenting where conhost or a task engine is collapsed into wermgr.exe as parent
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "-queue" and Grandparent in~ ("svchost.exe","taskhostw.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm ParentImage is System32\wermgr.exe and the child shell runs at SYSTEM/High integrity; capture the child command line and the wermgr.exe SHA256. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the SYSTEM shell and any children, and snapshot for forensics before restoring the signed wermgr.exe. 3) Hunt: correlate back to UC1 (MsMpEng.exe writing wermgr.exe) on the same host, review scheduled-task run history for Microsoft-Windows-WER, and sweep for lateral movement or credential dumping performed under the SYSTEM shell.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "wermgr.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\System32\"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessIntegrityLevel, Grandparent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\wermgr.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TokenElevationType, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: wermgr.exe Spawning Command Shell (RoguePlanet CVE-2026-50656 SYSTEM Escalation)
id: c1a97e05-3d4b-4f8a-8b21-9f7e2d6c4a83
description: System32 wermgr.exe spawning cmd/powershell indicates execution of the RoguePlanet payload as SYSTEM via the Windows Error Reporting scheduled task.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-patches-rogueplanet-defender.html
  - https://www.rescana.com/post/cve-2026-50656-microsoft-defender-rogueplanet-zero-day-enables-local-privilege-escalation-on-fully-patched-windows-10-11

    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
